maintopic: POST OFFICE ACT AMENDMENT.

speechtext: Mr. LEMIEUX moved for leave to introduce Bill (No. 104) to amend paragraph (1) of section 2 and paragraphs (n) and (o) of section 9 of the Post Office Act. He said: The object of this Bill is to introduce in the larger post offices of the country a new device called the self stamp selling box. It is a box by which any man, by putting in it a cent or a penny, can get his stamp of that denomination. At the same time, the use of this box saves to the department a large amount of money, as no commission has to be paid to any vendor of stamps. The box has been tried in two or three large post offices in Canada, and is found to be a great advantage to the public, especially in the rush season at Christmas time. It is used in Australia, where the invention was first taken out, and is also largely used in Europe. On the second reading of the Bill I will give fuller explanation.

maintopic: POST OFFICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: Is it the same kind of box that has been used in the Ottawa post office for some time ?

maintopic: POST OFFICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: I think there is one in the Ottawa post office.

maintopic: POST OFFICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext:
The minister, in his peregrinations, may not have heard of the incident that took place down at the Ottawa

post office. A young lady wanted a cent stamp, she put in her cent and the one cent stamp came out. But the blamed thing kept on turning out stamps one after the other, without additional money. It frightened the young lady, and she took to her heels and ran away. She made complaint, and I believe either the police or the engineering department was called in, and in due time they stopped the thing.

maintopic: POST OFFICE ACT AMENDMENT.
speechtext: The use of the box at first was an experiment, and there may have been something wrong with it. The hon. gentleman, I know, will be pleased to learn that one great advantage of this box is that it rejects all kinds of false coins.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the first time.

maintopic: RECIPROCITY-TRADE STATISTICS.
RECIPROCITY-TRADE STATISTICS.
speechtext: I would like to call -the attention of the Minister of Finance to a document which has been received from the United States by various members of parliament, a document issued, I suppose, by one of the departments of the administration at Washington. It is a most complete document; all the proceedings, all the data and a complete set of statistical tables are appended under one cover. It is a most important thing that full statistics should be in the hands of the members of parliament and available at as early a period as possible. I cannot think that the Minister of Finance has been a fortnight at these negotiations with efficient help with him, and that he has not had that basis or data for his negotiations that evidently, the United States Commissioners had very skillfully prepared and very full and comprehensive in all its parts. If the Minister of Finance had that, what reason in the world is there that the House has not been put in possession long before this of an equally comprehensive statement, The Minister of Finance seemed yesterday very unwilling to adopt a practice of the United States for fear that it might be unconstitutional here. I think the House would forgive him in that respect if he would give us something on a par or an equality with what the United States administration have given to their people.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: RECIPROCITY-TRADE STATISTICS.
speechtext:
My hon. friend has overlooked the fact that at the moment of presenting the matter to this House I laid on the table or made accessible to ' Hansard ' a somewhat elaborate statement containing comparisons which at the moment I thought probably covered all that any hon. member might desire. We had two most capable officials with us in Washington, .a most efficient staff, tout high as is my regard and esteem for these gentlemen, 87
I would not say they were equal to tlhe large army of officials which was available to our friends of the United States government, Day after day as incidents occurred in the negotiations they were able to turn the matter over to their army of officials, and they could have statistics prepared very much more elaborately 'than we could possibly expect to have within the same time. I quite agree, however, that it is desirable that the fullest possible information, and practically along the same lines should he given to this House ; our officers are now engaged in preparing it, and I will promise to expedite the return and see that it is laid before the House within a reasonable time before the discussion is resumed.

maintopic: RECIPROCITY-TRADE STATISTICS.
speechtext: Meanwhile, as it seems to be so difficult to have that done here, perhaps, through the kindly offices of the administration, we might toe aible to get a supply from Washington.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
maintopic: RECIPROCITY-TRADE STATISTICS.
speechtext: If my hon. friend thinks it desirable to have some extra copies of the statement prepared at Washington I would be happy to ask them to favour us in that respect, but I would thifik that the House would prefer to' have the information prepared by our own people. I think the House will agree that we are not to be blamed if we were not able to have more statistical information when we were so far away from home. We did have all the information which we thought necessary for an intelligent study of the subject but it could scarcely toe expected that after the negotiations were completed we could go to work and prepare the statistics while we were on our way back to Ottawa. There is no comparison between the two conditions. I will adopt my non. friend's suggestion, and ask our friends in Washington to give us some extra copies containing this information, tout I think the House would like also the information prepared by our own officials.

speechtext: My attention was called to an article in the Victoria ' Colonist ' from which I read this paragraph :

maintopic: CHINESE IMMIGRATION.
speechtext:
Mclnnes says that Sir Wilfrid Laurier told him that he contemplated the



possibility of doing away with the present restrictions on Chinese immigration.
I have no recollection at this moment of having discussed the matter with Mr. Mclnnes, tout I have no doubt that if he says so it is true because I discussed this matter not only with Mr. Mclnnes, if I did so, but with several parties when I was in British Columbia last summer, and since I came home also with different friends who take an interest in this question, not with the view, however, as stated toy Mr. Mclnnes of withdrawing the present restriction on Chinese immigration so as to make immigration from China absolutely free as it is from Europe, but I probably discussed with Mr. Mclnnes. and certainly with numerous parties, the advisability of abolishing our present legislation with regard to Chinese immigration, and if possible obtaining from the Chinese government such an arrangement as we have at the present time with the Japanese government which has wrorked admirably. The House is aware that we have at the present time an arrangement with the Japanese government whereby they undertook, some three or four years ago, themselves to restrict their own immigration to Canada to a certain figure. This arrangement has been faithfully carried out by the Japanese government and Japanese immigration has been kept, under the arrangement, constantly in check. At the present time, we have, and we have had for some twenty years on our statute-toook, a law which imposes a capitation tax upon every Chinaman coming into Canada. Last year the immigration suddenly went up to a pretty high figure, to something like 1,400 or 1,500. It is said that this 'was the result of frauds which had been committed, and the capitation tax is now the subject of an investigation in Vancouver. Whether there has been fraud or not I am still of the opinion that if it were possible to Obtain from the Chinese government such an arrangement as we have had with the Japanese government it would be far preferable. But, at the present moment, I have no recollection of discussing the matter with Mr. Mclnnes although it is quite possible I did so. I certainly discussed it with many other persons.

speechtext: Mr. KING moved the third reading of Bill (No. 97) to prohibit the improper use of opium and other drugs.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: PROHIBITION OF OPIUM AND OTHER DRUGS.
speechtext:
When this Bill was being considered in Committee of the Whole on Thursday evening last, some question was raised by my hon. friend from North Cape Breton (Mr. McKenzie) as to the propriety of the twelfth clause which provides that no conviction, judgment or order in respect of an offence against this Act shall be removed by certiorari, and the hon. gentleman said that he could not understand the Department of Justice giving the advice that such a provision should be inserted in the Bill. In view of what then took place, I wish to make an explanation that it was, I think, at my suggestion that this clause was inserted in the Bill by the Minister of Labour when the Bill was in preparation. Such a provision used to be of very considerable importance thirty

years ago before the courts possessed the power that has since been conferred upon them to amend technical defects in summary convictions. Hundreds and hundreds of convictions were quashed by the courts upon [DOT] technicalities where no question whatever existed but that the offence had been committed, and that the defendant had been justly convicted. The courts, however, at that time, possessed no power to make even the slightest correction or amendment in a conviction, which had to be dealt with, on its being removed by certiorari, in exactly the condition in which it came before the court; and, for that reason, I have no doubt, a provision of this character was very frequently inserted in Acts both of the imperial parliament, and of this parliament with a view to preventing justice being defeated by objections which had no merit, but which took advantage of some slip on the part of the convicting magistrate or of the person who had prepared the record of the conviction. The courts held, however, both in England and in this country, that notwithstanding such a clause in any statute, which, apparently, prohibits a court from issuing a certiorari to bring up a conviction, the courts still might do it if it could be seen that there was an absence of jurisdiction on the'part of the convicting magistrates to have entertained the complaint. The courts took the view that, in the absence of words clearly indicating the intention of parliament to take away this remedy which might be of the greatest use, the legislature could not have been supposed to have intended that the courts could not give relief if magistrates had acted in total absence of jurisdiction. So that the presence of such a clause never was an absolute prohibition against the courts reviewing the proceedings upon certiorari. Since the amendments which I have referred to have been made in our statutes, under which the most liberal power is now conferred upon the superior courts to correct technical mistakes in convictions which may be brought before them on certiorari, there is probably not very much value in a clause of this sort. But still it would have the legal effect of restricting the cases in which a convicted defendant would have the right to obtain certiorari to cases in which there was absence of jurisdiction on the part of the convicting magistrates. And, for that reason, when considering this measure, it seemed to me that it might be of use in furthering the purpose of the statute that such a provision should be inserted. And that was my reason for suggesting it to my hon. colleague the Minister of Labour. It is a provision which appears in the Canada Temperance Act, and which has been of effect in the history of the Canada Temperance Act t^ save from destruc-87}
tion a very great number of convictions where the defendant had no real merit in his effort to get rid of his fine or other punishment, but where, but for the existence of such a clause as this, the courts would have been compelled to quash the proceedings. This legislation is of very much the same character as the Canada Temperance Act, and it seemed to me that just in that view such a clause should be inserted in this Bill. But I wish to disclaim altogether the idea that I favour the presence of such a clause as a general thing in statutes which may be passed by this parliament creating criminal offences. I agree entirely in the views which were expressed by my hon. friend from North Cape Breton (Mr. McKenzie) when this Bill was in committee, that such a clause ought to be very sparingly used; and it was only because it seemed to me that the purpose of this Bill was of rather exceptional character that I recommended the insertion of the clause. There was another point in the committee which was more discussed. The hon. member for East Grey (Mr. Sproule) and the hon. member for St. Anne (Mr. Doherty) pointed out the objections which, undoubtedly, ordinarily would exist to delegating to the Governor in Council the right to make new offences, new crimes, by adding to the schedule of the statute. That objection was possibly cured in this [DOT]case by an amendment of the clause which delegates this power to the Governor in Council, an amendment made in the committee which limits the authority of the Governor in Council to add to the schedule the names of substances which may be derivatives or preparations of the drugs which by the Bill are prohibited, and, that amendment being made, I understood the objections to this particular clause or feature of the Bill were very much minimized, if not quite removed.
The hon. member for East Grey expressed a desire that, upon the third reading of the Bill, I should state my opinion with regard to that feature o'f the statute. And, while I do not think it is any question of law, I am willing to say, speaking simply as a member of this House, that I think such a course, while perfectly within the power of parliament, is one that ought to be very seldom and very sparingly taken.

maintopic: PROHIBITION OF OPIUM AND OTHER DRUGS.
speechtext:
The hon. gfentleman (Sir Allen Aylesworth) referred to the question raised about the desirability of the provision under section 14, that the Governor in Council shall have power to add to the number of substances, the possession, sale, or handling of which would, under such legislation, constitute a crime. I desire to say

and I think I made that clear the other evening-that there was no suggestion on my part that there was no

legal power to do this; but I did point out, what I am glad to see the minister finally recognizes, that it was very undesirable that a power in as wide terms as were set forth in the section originally, should be conferred on the Governor in Council to create a crime. The terms of the section, as originally introduced, were wide enough to make it possible for the government, without any intervention of the legislature whatever, to add any substance whatever to the schedule, and to make the possession or the handling of that substance a crime; and I think that before we got through, we were all pretty *well agreed that that was not a desirable kind of legislation. -But I never suggested, or wished to be understood as suggesting, that there was any question of the power of parliament to do this if it chose to do it.
Motion agreed to, and Bill read the third time and passed.

speechtext:
["Hear, hear.
Mr. FOSTER-and I will invite the hon. Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham), who looks serious enough just at this moment, to join with me in those prayers, is that a little more sensitiveness of conscience may be imparted to the members of the administration from the Prime Minister down to the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Pugsley) when those awful things are exposed to the House and when that publicity which is the guardian and the guarantee of private and public life sp eulogized by the Prime Minister to-night is fought for by this side and the door is banged and bolted on the other side of the House.
But, I am not going to leave this discussion without bringing forward just one further thought, and it is this: Outside of this particular instance as it affects the office and as it affects the man in the office and the canons of public and private life, there is a very grave consideration which none of us, I am sure, will leave out of account. It is the power of example. Of all men in the whole public service, that man who ought to be the most careful, that man who ought to be the most circumspect, that man who ought to avoid the least suspicion or comment is the min-

ister of the department and the minister of the government who is to set an example to the whole public service and to the public life of this country. What would we think to-morrow morning if the customs collector in the port of Montreal, were to have had a meeting of his friends and admirers in the city of Montreal, and they had subscribed a testimonial of $50,000, had had a banquet and had all this beautiful publicity, tout had failed to give the names of the subscribers and it went out through the length and breadth of this country that the collector of customs in the port of Montreal had received gifts from his friends and admirers ? What would the public opinion say ? Is it not proper for me, knowing the collector of customs in Montreal, to say, that, in my opinion, he is not rich and that he is honest? If, because a man is poor and honest in the case of a minister of the Crown is a reason why the sound canons of political morality should be violated, what reason is there that the collector of customs, a sub-officer under the Crown, should not take from his friends and admirers, on the ground that he is poor and honest, a testimonial, because this is the sange reason as that which is given why .ministers should accept it ? If the Minister of Finance may take $120,000 from his friends and admirers, why cannot the Minister of Public Works take $120,000 from his friends and admirers ? But I will venture this that if to-morrow morning the news went out through this country that the friends and admirers of the Minister of Public Works had given him a secret donation of $100,000 there would be ructions in this country. When the example is set, when the principle is formed and the practise is laid down in the case of one minister of the Crown, how are you going to prevent other ministers of the Crown from following it, and in exactly the same way the pernicious influence goes through the whole service and permeates the whole country. Your sub-officer or under officer, if you may speak of him as such, says:	Well, the high muck-a-mucks take
these gifts from their friends and admirers because they are poor and honest* I am poor-mighty poor-and I am just as honest as they are; why cannot I take a little gift on the side too, without any unnecessary publicity ?
I have not the least doubt in the world that demoralization, swift and sure, along the whole _ line follows this unfortunate movement in the wrong direction. To-night we find the Prime Minister with his party behind him, and this latest advocate closing the debate on that side, declaring that it is perfectly right for ministers of the Crown to take gifts if only they are poor and honest. Have any other members of the government taken gifts?-(Don't all speak at once!)-
Is the Prime Minister a sinner in that respect? Would that make his feelings kind towards the Minister of Finance? Are any other ministers in similar positions for lesser sums? How soon this will spread, how far it will go, now that the supreme sanction of the Prime Minister and the Liberal party is given to the reversal of the law and rule of parliament which has existed for twenty years against it and which tonight they propose to abolish, leaving this matter wide, wide open.

maintopic: SUPPLY-MR. J. A. MACDONALD AND RECIPROCITY.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before you leave the Chair, I am pleased to state that I observe by yesterday's 1 Globe ' that the editor of that journal has been fully restored to his wonted vigour. On the front page of that paper there is a long telegram from him which shows that whatever rumours may have been around the country to the contrary, he is in possession of his usual mental faculties. However, I regret that I am called upon again to dispute some of the positions that gentleman has taken. I would not refer to the matter but that this is the-first occasion on -which he has appeared in the arena directly. The ' Globe ' editorial, referring to the public says:
To them it may be necessary to say that the editor of the 'Globe' has not at any time or under any circumstances made an arrangement with any person under which he agreed to advocate any fiscal policy as lending itself specially to the cause of universal peace.
I never said that he did ' agree ' to it, Sir. What I did say was that Dr. Starr-Jordan and Mr. Macdonald and those other gentlemen, whether they agreed to it or not, are actually doing it, and I proved it the other day by reference to Dr. Starr-Jordan's own speeches here-that while preaching peace, they were at the same time preaching reciprocity between Canada and the United States along lines which could only have one termination, that is, the annexation of this country to the'United States. Mr. Macdonald's telegram, after a long newspaper extract, in which is used Mr. DOHERTY.
the term * reciprocity ' instead of the term ' peace society,' is as follows:
San Diego, Cal., Jan. 29.-The statement published as having been made at St. Catharines by Col. -Sam Hughes is absolutely false in every essential particular.
I will prove before I am through that it is true in every particular.
I neither was sent nor did I go to Washington in connection with the reciprocity question.
I will show further on that he is quibbling and equivocating on the word ' reciprocity.'
If Col. Hughes cares to know, salaries double the amount he mentions have been offered to me for regular professional services, but never a dollar for any purpose he named.
I am very much surprised, knowing Mr. Macdonald's character, that he has not taken advantage of these large salaries.
In association with President David Starr-Jordan of Leland Stanford University, John R. Mott and others, I am a member of the board of directors of the 'World's Peace Foundation,' established by Mr. Ginn for promoting in every civilized country the settlement of all international disputes by judicial arbitration and not by war. Necessary expenses are paid, -but no director is under salary or makes gain financially.'
We will discuss that later on.
Reciprocity is not on the programme.
Then, why did they put it on?
Tariffs are a matter of no concern.
Then why is the discussion of tariffs foisted on this country by Dr. Starr-Jordan and others?
The task is much more serious. It is to direct the national systematic awakening and organizing of public opinion in every civilized nation on the question of the demoralizing curse of war, and the intolerable folly of increased armaments. We advocate the substitution of independent arbitration as at The Hague.
Neither the founder nor any of the directors favours the political union of Canada and the United States. Personally and in the interests of world peace, I oppose any change in Canada's imperial relations. As a free nation in the empire, Canada can exercise greater influence than is possible through independence. Col. -Sam Hughes' statement is a 'wholecloth' falsehood. Only a slanderer and a coward will repeat it after this.
Well, Sir, I am here to prove that I have not mis-stated a single word, and that I am neither a slanderer nor a coward. Mr. Macdonald has attained to that mental condition wherein the spirit of selfishness, insane ambition and tyranny bordering on a sense of divine right, has become domination, a mental condition which is never found in any of the great men who, like

him, profess to be followers of ' the Meek and Lowly One nor in any of the great editors of the great journals of the country; but it is common among the inferior class of clergymen in all churches, and among the inferior editors generally. I need not again repeat my assertions, Sir, further than to put them in consecutive order, to show that neither Mr. Macdonald nor the ' Globe ' has directly or indirectly attempted to meet my charges.
I stated, first, that Mr. Macdonald went to Washington either on his own personal account or as the confidential agent of this government to conduct reciprocity negotiations.	This Mr. Macdonald technically
denies. I re-affirm it, however, and will prove him to be a deceiver and equivoca-tor.
My next charge was that Mr. Macdonald is not now paid a full salarv or for full time as editor of that great oracle of truth, righteousness and fair dealing, the Toronto ' Globe ', but is paid for only part of his time by the ' Globe '.
My third charge was that for part of his time Mr. Macdonald is in receipt of salary, or expenses, or rake-off, or income, or solatium, or indemnity, or consolation, or alleviation, or balm, or any other word that would fill the bill, from the fund largely provided bv Mr. Ginn, of Boston, named the ' Peace Societv Fund ', such ' balm ' being in the form of golden Yankee eagles, or their equivalent. These three statements were made by me first in St. Catharines on an open public platform. I knew that there would be some coward garbed as a ' Globe ' editor, or some despicable colleague of Mr. Macdonald, imbued with the same spirit of persecution and hypocrisy, shielding himself behind a five cent white necktie and attaining notice not by his personal worth or godliness or ability, but by the atmosphere of superstition and tolerance surrounding him-one of that fry mat bring the sacred name of religion into disrepute; one failing to follow the maxim and practice of the Master as aptly put by Chaucer:
Christ's lore and His apostles twelve lie preached,
But first he followed it himself.
. -one despised by every capable godly minister of the gospel, as well as by every honest citizen and newspaper editor ;-I knew that some such ignorant person would charge me with shielding myself behind the privileges of parliament. Therefore I made the charge first openly on the public platform at St. Catharines, and subsequently in the House. Yet I have been told that one of this tribe, no longer ago than Sunday in the city of Ottawa, in the pulpit of one of the churches here, charged me with shielding myself behind the privileges of parliament in this matter. I am informed that this is the same gentleman who, when an election was being held in the city of Ottawa, a few years ago, went with his five cent necktie on, and pledged himself to a member of the Conservative party that he was sick and tired of the ' rascally Ross government ' in Toronto and would do his utmost to turn it out: yet when the leader of this same ' rascally government ', the Hon. George W. Ross, appeared in Ottawa, the foremost heeler in the gang who paid honour to him was this same individual.
And he would do his utmost to turn them out. Inside of a very few days this same leader of that ' rascally government in Toronto,' the Hon. G. W. Ross, appeared on the public platform in Ottawa, and the foremost heeler in the gang which surrounded him, was this same individual. On another occasion in that same election, in order to still better carry out the plans of the Grit party, this individual- I shall not disgrace the sacred calling of the ministry by calling him a clergyman-: attempted to bring this man Macdonald, the editor of the ' Globe ' from Toronto to preach in his pulpit on the Sunday before the election, so that he might try and convince the congregation of the aggregation of virtue of which that good government was composed; but to the credit of the congregation, they refused to allow Mr. Macdonald into the pulpit. Not content with that, this same parson took a list of the members of his congregation and marked -I do not know in what colour-how they might be influenced to vote or how they might be disposed to vote, and he did this for the Grit heelers of the party in Ottawa so that they might use it for election purposes. This is the gentleman who is backing up Mr. Macdonald.
In his lecture before the Canadian Club on Saturday, and in his sermon on Sunday, Prof. Starr-Jordan said that if we could only do away with the custom house officers, that would be an ideal condition between the two countries. Yet Mr. Macdonald will claim that these peace society speakers are not meddling in reciprocity. Mr. Macdonald's next statement was that he never was sent, nor did he go to Washington in connection with the reciprocity question. But he is quibbling with the word ' reciprocity.' What is the meaning of reciprocity ? He will not deny that he went to Washington in order to bring about negotiations for a change in the United States tariff which would do away with the maximum clause trouble. We wanted to induce the United States not to enforce that maximum clause and Canada humiliated itself by making certain changes. That was the kind of reciprocity that Mr. Macdonald wanted to bring about. .The

meaning of reciprocity is: 1st. Mutual action and reaction; 2nd. Reciprocal advantages, obligations or rights. His next statement was that he was associated with Prof. Starr-Jordan-rather an unfortunate admission after the speech of Prof. Jordan, deliberately advocating reciprocity-and that only his expenses were paid by the peace society, I have it on good authority that he gets a pretty large sum from this society every year and he dare not deny it.
Mr. Macdonald says that reciprocity is not on the programme of the society. Why is it not ? It certainly looms out largely in the speeches of the oracles of that society. He speaks also of the demoralizing curse of war, but inasmuch as my hon. friend from Algoma is anxious to take the floor, I shall not touch that aspect of the case now, but defer dealing with it until another occasion. In speaking of war, Mr. Macdonald reminds me of the small boy who said to his father: You had better give up cussing or leave the church. In like manner, Mr. Macdonald, had better show a little more Christian spirit if he intends continuing in that great cause, the promotion of peace among nations. In this connection, I cannot refrain from quoting the words of Eliza Cook
Never trust the soft breathing that preaches of peace
With a smile on the lips and a tear in the eye-
Hear it all with good will blit be provident still,
With men that are earnest and powder that is dry.
In Dante's Inferno, we are told, that in one of the nethermost regions below there are a tremendous number of gentlemen who parade clothed in pure and spotless white-I do not know whether they are members of the peace society or not-but they wear a rueful aspect, the lining of their garments is the heaviest lead and the road they have to travel is rough, rocky and jagged. These are the hypocrites who once defaced human society. I sincerely hone that so great an evil will not befall this editor of the ' Globe.' Might I be allowed as a layman, to express the wish that he may not be found in this company in this nethermost region in the future. Therefore I would respectfully suggest that some steps be taken to reclaim him-and in that connection, I would do my best to bring him back to what he should be-namely, an open, square man, and have him give up equivocating to the extent he has been practising that art for some considerable time.

speechtext:
Before you leave the Chair, Mr. Speaker, for Mr. HUGHES.
the House to go into Committee of Supply, I desire to refer as briefly as possible to a matter respecting which I gave notice last Monday, 'and which was discussed during the latter part of last session. At the close of my remarks I shall offer a resolution on the subject, which, I feel satisfied, from the manner in which it will be offered, and the principle it emphasizes, cannot fail to meet with the approval of both sides from the right hon. gentleman down. At the outset let me say that this is not a motion of want of confidence so that hon. gentlemen opposite need have no qualms of conscience about accepting it if they feel so disposed. All I desire is to intercept the House, on jthe motion to go into Supply, for the short time necessary to consider the principle involved in the resolution I am about to offer. This resolution lays down the principle advocated by the Liberal party-some twenty years ago, and which, in the public interest, it is necessary should now again be discussed. This necessity arises from recent occurrences which call for the application of that principle. I refer to the principle involved in the accepting by cabinet ministers of testimonials in the shape of gifts of money.
In whatever I have to say, I desire this to be distinctly understood, that in bringing this matter to the attention of the House I have no intention of injuring any public man.

speechtext:
Yes, I expected that jeer, but I do desire to emphasize this fact that the necessity for what observations I have" now to offer to Jthis House, the necessity for the resolution I propose shortly to place in your hands, emphasizing that position, is laid at the doors and attributable to the right hon. the Prime Minister of this government; to him and to him alone, because, Sir, niine months ago in this House, as was my privilege, and my duty as a public man, I moderately and temperately, and I think in 'no objectionable manner, dTew to his attention certain facts and certain principles applicable to those facts, and what did I get

from the right hon. gentleman, but sneers and contumely? I desire now to emphasize those principles and to draw this matter to the attention of the House for the second time, in the manner in which a great principle affirmed unanimously by this House in 1891 should be again repeated and emphasized. The principle announced, struggled for, claimed as a great victory by the Liberal party in 1891 has been departed from in 1910, and is in danger of being departed from again in 1911; to emphasize further my desire as to the need of a rigid adherence to these principles by asking the House to accept the resolution which I will move at the conclusion of my remarks, a copy of which has already been placed in the hands of the Prime Minister. Sir, the resolution which I shall place in your hands is based upon one of twenty years ago. On August 13, 1891, the right hon. Sir Richard Cartwright, then a prominent member of the opposition of this House moved the following resolution on going into Supply and not as a vote of want of confidence:
That Mr. Speaker do not now leave the chair, but that it be resolved: That the acceptance of gifts or testimonials of any kind on the part of ministers of the Crown or of any member of their families from contractors, government officials or other persons having pecuniary relations with the government, is entirely opposed to sound principles of administration, and is calculated to bring parliamentary government into contempt, and that the example thus given tends to corrupt and demoralize the officials serving under ministers who have accepted or permitted the acceptance of gifts or testimonials as aforesaid.
I shall ask the House to reiterate and reaffirm these words in the light of recent events, and I cannot help noticing that at the time that resolution was passed, lodged as it was against the late Sir John A. Macdonald as well as others, lodged against members of the family of that right hon. gentleman toy my right hon. friend the Prime Minister, Sir John Macdonald had hardly been two months in his grave. Yet my right hon. friend on the 3rd of May last, and his friends now, can jeer and treat me with contumely because I endeavoured, as is my public duty, to refer moderately to that resolution and to express my desire not to go beyond the limits of what would be proper in dealing with a subject inviting such delicate and proper treatment. I have no desire to injure any public man; I am not here for that purpose and I say no one can truthfully say that there is any attempt in referring to this matter to detract from any prestige which the friends of my hon. friend the Minister of Finance are of opinion he has gained by recent events, meaning the negotiations at Washington. I brought this matter to the attention of the
House on May 3 last, and gave notice of my intention to discuss this matter before the return of the Finance Minister from Washington, and when on the day I expected my hon. friend to be in the House I found he was not, I postponed the discussion until he should return. In all that I say about my friend, the Minister of Finance, I spehk after due notice, and I am glad to say in his presence. I say it when his friends laud him, and I am not going to say improperly-think, he is erect in public opinion, when he is in the eyes of the whole commercial world, when his followers believe him to be strong in the confidence of the people.

speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: SUPPLY-MR. J. A. MACDONALD AND RECIPROCITY.
subtopic: TESTIMONIALS TO MINISTERS OF THE CROWN.
speechtext:
The full disclosure now by the Minister of Finance or by the right hon. the Prime Minister of facts and circumstances long withheld from this HOuse and this country can form the only justification of this transaction, and further withholding of information which it is of the utmost importance that this House and this country should have, can only avoid one unfortunate circumstance and that is that grave suspicion must hang over a minister of the Crown of this country.
Let us discuss for a moment the manner in which the resolution of Sir Richard Cartwright was supported. The right hon. the Minister of Trade and Commerce in this government, then a prominent member of the opposition, spoke to the resolution as follows: at page 3829 of the ' Hansard * of 1891:
You cannot by possibility-and every man knows that I speak the truth-you cannot by possibility allow a minister of the state to accept gifts of any kind, without, if the practice becomes known, demoralizing in a very high degree the whole society over which he presides.
Those are not my words, those are the words of a minister high in the confidence of this government, of an hon. minister presiding over a very important part of this government, the Department of Trade and Commerce.
At page 3831 of the same ' Hansard,' Sir Richard Cartwright said:
I have observed, Sir, that some of the hon. gentleman's apologists have undertaken to mitigate the error, or the crime, call it what you will, which was committed by the reception of that testimonial under the circumstances, by the plea, which I think was also advanced in the other case, that the hon. gentleman did not know who had subscribed to his testimonial. Such a plea, in my judgment, is a direct aggravation of the offence. A public minister has no right whatever to allow any gift to be made to him unless it is done publicly, and unless he knows from what sources it proceeds; and, Sir, I would say this, that if a minister of the Crown tells

me that he has accepted a gift, not knowing and not choosing to know from whom it proceeded, so far from regarding such a plea as a mitigation, I say that such a plea raises a presumption of guilt. It was his duty to know it; it was his duty to find out; it was Iris duty to see that not one penny went into his pockets or into his coffers unless it came from such sources that he could honourably and fairly receive it.
Now, Sir, the leader of the opposition of that day, who is now the Prime Minister of this country, in the same debate, made use of these words -which I quote from page 3840.
The Minister of Justice said a moment ago in reference to the testimonial offered to the honourable Minister of Public Works, the member for Three Rivers, that that hon. gentleman did not know who were the subscribers. Sir, if he did not know, why did he not look at the list? If the hon. gentleman did not know, it was because he choose to remain ignorant of who were the names on the list, and if he chose to be ignorant of the names which are on the list, is it not because his moral sense told him that he might there find names of persons giving contributions which could not be accepted at all? Is it not simply because his conscience told him that if he were to look at that list he would find there the names of men who were every day supplicants in his office for favours? That is the reason why the honourable Minister of Public Works did not choose to have a look at that list. If that is not the reason why did he choose to he blind on that matter? Then, I call upon hon. gentlemen opposite to tell what is the reason, if there could he any good reason for it. Certainly there could be nothing wrong in the admirers of a man in public life coming to his help and rescuing him; hut it seems to me that the recipient of such favours would he naturally too glad to know who are the persons to whom he owes gratitude, and if he does not choose to know who are those to whom he owes gratitude, it must he because his moral sense tells him that he would find there names which would he a ccndemnation of his accepting such a testimonial.
Sir, these are not my words, they are not the words of any gentleman on this side of the House, they are the words of the present Prime Minister of Canada who is sitting at the right hand of the Minister of Finance. But in conjunction with a testimonial involving the gift of a large sum of money, said to be as much as $120,000, presented last April or May to the Finance Minister, let us see what *was said by the party organs with regard to it, and let us see how much it is in line with what my right hon. friend the Prime Minister said on that occasion. The Ottawa ' Free Press,' the government organ in this city, published the day after the testimonial was presented, made this remark ;
The list of donors is anonymous, and Mr. Fielding is made aware only of the fact that Mr. BOYCE.
the future of himself and his family is provided for.
My right hon. friend says there is only one justification, namely, that there is a list, and that the list is made public ; that if a public man chooses to accept a testimonial in the shape of a gift of money, and chooses not to look at the list, it must *be because his moral sense tells him that he would find on it the names of the men who ought not to -be there. That is the position. In view, therefore, of the fact that the Minister of Finance did, early in the spring of 1910, receive a large testimonial in the shape of a sum of money amounting to a fortune, without knowing who contributed it, the case falls directly under the condemnation of the right hon. gentleman who leads this House. The testimonial,\if we are to understand aright what the right hon. gentleman said on the 3rd day of May last in this House, was accepted ; it was accepted in the presence of the right hon. gentleman the Prime Minister of this country who was himself present, agreed to, approved of, and applauded the giving of that testimonial, entirely in contravention of the words and the principles which he had laid down in 1891. Yet there has been no list of the donors made public, and there was a statement, not denied by my right hon. friend, that the Minister of Finance did not know who the donors were. I do not say, Mr. Speaker,
I do not desire to be understood as saying, that under all circumstances and conditions the friends of a cabinet minister may not, in his hour of need, come to his rescue, and in their enthusiasm and admiration for the services he has rendered in a public capacity, make that provision for ' him which his devotion to the pressing cares of state has made it impossible for him to provide for himself. This principle was laid down by the present Prime Minister when speaking to the resolution of the 13th, of August, 1891, and I will again run the risk of wearying the House with a short quotation from page 3840 of the ' Hansard ':
Of course, in the matter of this testimonial, it is an act absolutely indifferent in itself. It may he wrong or it may he good, according to circumstances, but if such an act is done in the open light of day, then, Sir, it is the best prohibition that there can he against any wrong taking place.
I have the utmost sympathy, Mr. Speaker, for any public man who, having devoted the best years of his earning power to the service of his country, finds himself, when the years are crowding upon him, in a state of embarrassed circumstances, which contribute their bitterness to the weight of his care. But I say that public men, especially ministers of the Crown, must realize that gifts of money to releive their embarrassment must only

be accepted under the most stringent safeguards of public honour and national integrity, the most important of which, as has been said, is absolute publicity to the light of day, letting the people know who furnished the funds constituting that testimonial, letting them see that nothing 'is concealed, that there wab nothing wrong, that everything is open to the broad light of day, before all men. Sir, those were the facts before the public of this country prior to the 3rd day of May, 1910, facts which, as I have stated, were banded about in the public newspapers of this country prior to that date- except of course the facts which have taken place since. And how was I then not justified, on the third day of May, 1910, in referring to that matter in this House, with an idea of doing what? Of criticising the Finance Minister? No, Sir, I defy any hon. gentleman opposite to say that the remarks I made on the 3rd of May, 1910, were not offered in a fair and reasonable spirit, that they were not moderate and temperate remarks, and I say they called for a more dignified reception than that accorded them by the right hon. the Prime Minister. I asked the right hon. gentleman if there was a list, I asked the right hon. gentleman whether he would produce that list, I asked him to name the services for which the testimonial was granted; and the right hon. gentleman scornfully and satirically characterized my inquiry as ' curiosity,' curiosity which he emphasized by repeating the word twice. Now, Sir, the Prime Minister's reply, on the 3rd May last, is worthy of some consideration by this House, in view of the circumstances in bygone years when, as leader of the opposition, he was declaiming against the Conservative party. The right hon. gentleman commenced by emphasizing the manifest and undoubted integrity of the Minister of Finance. Who doubted the integrity of the Minister of Finance? I certainly never did. There was no remark made by me which would cast any aspersion on the Minister of Finance. I have no desire now to cast any aspersion upon the integrity of the Minister of Finance further than the right hon. gentleman cast upon him himself by attempting _ to derogate from his honour by placing a shield where the rays of the sunlight of day ought ever to be falfing on a public man. The right hon. gentleman said on that occasion that the friends of Mr. Fielding came to him and that the reply that he gave them was that ' There is nothing too good for Fielding,' to use his own words.

speechtext: Hear, hear.

speechtext: We think so still.

maintopic: SUPPLY-MR. J. A. MACDONALD AND RECIPROCITY.
subtopic: TESTIMONIALS TO MINISTERS OF THE CROWN.
speechtext:
I have no doubt. The right hon. the Prime Minister, under certain other circumstances said of another minister of the Crown that he was prouder of him than ever. The Prime Minister did not stipulate that there should be a public list, he did not lay down any of the precautions that Shis resolution and his remarks in support of his resolution of the 13th of August, 1891, called for. He did not provide that there should be a list, that that list should be open to the light of day, and to the public and that it should be approved of by the Minister of Finance himself. The Prime Minister made a statement on his own responsibility that no one had subscribed to that list whose name ought not to be there. On page 8791 of * Hansard ' of last session, the right hon. gentleman says that:
The money came from private sources.
Of course it did. It did not come from the public treasury-it was not as bad as that.
The money came from private sources; that I assert on my honour as a man, on my responsibility as the Prime Minister of Canada.
The right hop. gentleman, having pledged his responsibility as the Prime Minister of Canada, that this money came from private sources, is unable to tell me, in referring to the newspaper report that the Dominion Steel Company had contributed, where the money came from because he says that he does not know whether the company contributed or not. There is a remarkable contrast, the remarkable state of things with regard to a very important subject in which a very large principle is involved. May I ask the right hon. gentleman what he meant when he said that upon his honour as a man and upon his responsibility as the Prime Minister of this country he could assert that this money came from private sources, that not one dollar was subscribed by any person who ought not to have subscribed and why he should also say in the same speech and almost in the same breath when asked if the Dominion Steel Company had subscribed, that he had no personal knowledge? With regard to the Dominion Steel Company, he said :
I do not believe there is a word of truth in it. At all events, if such an institution as that had been allowed to subscribe, it would be a gross breach of the understanding which was arrived at when Mr. Fielding's testimonial was started.
How does the right hon. gentleman square one statement with the other? How can he pledge his honour as a man and his responsibility as Prime Minister in answering a very important question upon a very important principle, pledging himself and committing himself to a certain statement,

while, with regard to another subscription, saying that he does not know whether it is so or not and that if it is so it should not be allowed? Therefore, I say in criticism further of the hon. gentleman's attitude on May 3 last, that he did not deal fairly, with me or with this House, or with this country with regard to this question, and I leave it to the judgment of the House in view of what I have just quoted as to whether the right hon. gentleman did or did not. Why should the right hon. gentleman side-track the information in that way? Why should he pledge his responsibility and a moment afterwards confess that he had not personal knowledge upon which to base the responsibility that he pledged before the House on this important matter? On May 3, 1910, I asked for the production of the list and I will just quote from page 8789 of ' Hansard ' of that date the concluding words of the remarks that I then offered to the House:
I shall not attempt to dwell upon the principles involved nor to moralize upon the dangers of the situation, but I feel safe in assuming that my right hon. friend, realizing that he spoke upon this resolution in 1891, and that he congratulated his party upon the signal victory obtained, will see that the grand victory of which he speaks, and which was attained as he would argue through blood and tears, be not besmirched now in 1910 by a derogation from the principles then enunciated. The only way, as I submit, in which my hon. friend can put himself square with the resolution, the only way in which I submit he can discharge the duty he owes to this country as Prime Minister and leader of the government, is to make full disclosure, and publish the names and lay the list on the fable.
The Prime Minister, in effect, declined to do that, did absolutely nothing, took no action, made no statement to the effect that the list should he published, although the list was in existence, absolutely departed from the resolution of 1891 and* from all the principles which he enunciated in support of that resolution. Why has there not been a statement since that time ? A testimonial of so large a sum of money as $120,000, a fortune, presented to a minister of the Crown in secrecy, subscribed by persons whose names are absolutely withheld on the demand of this House-why is there this secrecy ? Can the right hon. gentleman now offer to this House or the country any excuse whatever for withholding the names of those who subscribed to that testimonial, for withholding since that time the testimonial which was given and will the right hon. gentleman now offer to the House any reasonable excuse why the list has not been made public which was demanded on the 3rd May, 1910. I would be very glad indeed to have an answer from the right hon. gentleman. Mr. Mr. BOYCE.
Speaker, I have offered to take my seat end give the right hon. gentleman the floor in order that he might reply to a question which, when he was in opposition, he thundered at the then government, and, Sir, he is speechless. Then, Sir, I hurl my right hon. friend's words back in his teeth, though twenty long years have rolled by since he uttered them. There being a list -and he has admitted that there is a list -and the Minister of Finance not knowing the names of those on the list, then I say to my right hon. friend (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) that the words I have just quoted from his speech with regard to moral sense, rectitude and public integrity are borne out, and he, and he alone, under these circumstances, must bear the onus and the odium. What condition of things has he brought about ? What do we find the newspapers saying regarding our public men ? How have the newspapers been reviling the Minister of Finance in a way that no man in private life would tolerate for one half hour. Here I extract firm the St. John 'Standard' of the 20th of January

speechtext: A bad authority.

maintopic: SUPPLY-MR. J. A. MACDONALD AND RECIPROCITY.

speechtext: I am not saying what kind of newspapers these are, but that any kind of newspapers

maintopic: SUPPLY-MR. J. A. MACDONALD AND RECIPROCITY.
subtopic: TESTIMONIALS TO MINISTERS OF THE CROWN.
speechtext: That is in a class by itself.

maintopic: SUPPLY-MR. J. A. MACDONALD AND RECIPROCITY.
subtopic: TESTIMONIALS TO MINISTERS OF THE CROWN.
speechtext:
And you are in a class by yourself. In the front page of this newspaper, the St. John 'Standard,' is a flaring headline with these words: 'Mr. Fielding got stolen money.' A nice statement for the right hon. Prime Minister to make it possible to publish in any newspaper ! Will the Prime Minister suggest that any newspaper in this broad Dominion would have the audacity to make such a statement concerning a public man had the Prime Minister given to this country the list of contributors to this fund? Or will he suggest that the editor wfho made such a statement could have remained outside a jail ? Why, it would have been a criminal libel of the most outrageous character, and the newspaper would have been utterly without defence to it, if the Prime Minister had been true to his pledges and to these great principles that he enunciated. This article and others, published in the press throughout the length and breadth of the Dominion, declare that it is reported upon high authority that Wm. E. Travers, late general manager of the Farmers' Bank -now under sentence of six years' imprisonment for stealing money from the bank, falsifying government returns, which led to a terrible financial catastrophe in the shape of a bank failure-had contributed to this testimonial the sum of $2,500. And who, I ask, is responsible for that state-

mentP Who but the Prime Minister of Canada is responsible for the fact that it is possible for anybody to say that Travers, or Sheldon of Montreal, or any other person has contributed a dollar to this testimonial ? I give my right hon. friend this *warning for what it may be worth-that he has gone a step too far. In departing from his principles, in his hysterical effort to cloak and cover up this transaction in which his Minister of Finance is concerned, he has brought down upon his colleague very severe criticism and very grave suspicion under which, unless this list be published, I fear the Minister of Finance -by reason of the action of the Prime Minister-will suffer for some time. Here is the evening ' Capital ' of Saskatoon. I do not know what kind of a paper it is-

maintopic: SUPPLY-MR. J. A. MACDONALD AND RECIPROCITY.
subtopic: TESTIMONIALS TO MINISTERS OF THE CROWN.
speechtext: It is a Tory paper.

maintopic: SUPPLY-MR. J. A. MACDONALD AND RECIPROCITY.
subtopic: TESTIMONIALS TO MINISTERS OF THE CROWN.
speechtext:
I do not take responsibility for the statements of these papers; I merely indicate what is printed in them to let the public know that the Prime Minister and he alone is responsible for what they say. This is one of the few instances in which one can saddle the Prime Minister with full responsibility for what is published in a Conservative newspaper. In the evening ' Capital ' of Saskatoon, of January 20, instant, appears this heading, ' Convicted bank manager said to have contributed to Fielding testimonial.' Now, I ask the Prime Minister, in all sincerity and earnestness, and realizing the gravity of what that means-and no one knows how intense is the gravity of a personal character for the hon. gentleman about whom it is said-why does not he relieve his friend the Minister of Finance from his lying under an imputation so gross, so awful so criminal as this, when to do so he has only to stick to his principles and publish this list?
It has been suggested that all sorts of people have contributed to that testimonial. My right hon. friend has seen, as I have, the names of different persons given as contributors to this testimonial, persons occupying high positions in this country, many of whom have pecuniary relations with the government in one department or another, but especially with the department of the Finance Minister, almost every day of their commercial lives. Is it fair, is it just, is it in accord with the principle that my right non. friend laid down, that it should be possible that such a statement as that should go out to the public, yet not be brought into this House and denied when by that statement a minister of the Crown is laid under grave suspicion?
I need not mention names of those who, it is said, contributed. It is advisable not to do so in the absence of their verification. I do not know the number of them, although I might give him greater evidence than possibly he thinks I may be able to give with regard to these names. But I say it is not my intention in this debate to indulge in personalities, or to implicate one person more than another. I desire merely to emphasize those grand and noble principles, which my right hon. friend on the 13th of August, 1891, hailed with delight as the achievement of a magnificent principle, a principle long fought for by the Liberal party in this House, and long denied by the then Conservative government, which principle at last, owing to the arguments brought forward and the tactics employed by my right hon. friend as leader of the opposition, they were forced to concede in the interests of purity of government. If that testimonial, in the shape of the gift of a fortune, were given and accepted in the manner and under the circumstances set out in the newspapers of the day, and in the newspapers which have been publishing accounts of it in the last nine months, I say that the giving of it and the acceptance of if would be a brazen defiance of the first principles of parliamentary government, of the resolution of this House, of the pronounced views of the present ministry, including _ the present Prime Minister and the Minister of Trade and Commerce, and of all decent and honest practice which should characterize public men.
That a public man occupying so high a position should toe allowed, and should be led into-because that is the way I prefer to put it, as I fancy my hon. friend engineered the whole deal-led into the position in which he now finds his minister, an absolutely inextricable position, from which there is no outlet except that which he provided for himself in 1891, the publication of the list, is a most startling fact to put before this House, and the country, and I say that if he persists in that position, it is a disgrace to our public men and a tolot on this administration, a blot possibly darker and more flagrant than any of the dark blots which have characterized it. Sir, we have charged in this House since 1896 different scandals against this government. We have charged that under this government there is the reign of the middleman, and the grafter, dishonesty in public affairs, and wantoness in the expenditure of public money. If the Prime Minister clouds this thing with a cloak of secrecy in defiance of his own principles enunciated in this House, it is a fitting climax to the carnival of graft and corruption that has characterized his administration. I ask my right hon. friend now, where did the money come from? I do not ask it lightly ; I ask it in all seriousness ; because he repeated that question himself

in this House in May, 1910, and then gave an answer on his responsibility as Prime Minister of Canada which, if a six-year-old boy bad given at school, he would have been whipped. He first said that the money had come from private sources, and then he said he did not know where it had come from except one subscription which was charged, but if it had come from that source, it -was wrong. I am entitled to know, every member of this House is entitled to know, every taxpayer in this country, man, woman and child, is entitled to know, where that money came from. I am here to know-I am here to demand- I believe this House is entitled to demand- where that money came from ; and if the Prime Minister will awake to a realization of the position in which he has placed this country, and one of his ministers, he will see that it is of the utmost importance to this House and this country, for him now to tell where that money came from. 1 ask my right hon. friend. another question here and now : Can a minister of state accept gifts of money privately subscribed, withholding the list of subscribers, and unhold the dignity of the Crown which he serves as a minister? I ask my right hon. friend to answer ; if he will, I will be glad to give place to him.

Sir, my right hon. friend is great at quotations. Sometimes he likes to quote the blunt and rugged honesty of the words of the late Hon. George Brown. My right hon. friend is quite an admirer of the writings, and the position taken by that late hon. gentleman on certain great questions. I want now, for the benefit of my right hon. friend particularly, and for the benefit of this House, to quote to him words of the late Hon. George Brown with which I have no doubt he is very familiar :
If, Sir, a public man avows certain principles, agitates those principles and seeks to overthrow the government of the day and establishes those principles, and if when he attains power he laughs at his principles and casts his professions to the winds, he is aiming a blow at public morality.
Shades of George Brown, Mr. Speaker! When the right hon. gentleman cannot rise in his place in this House and affirm a principle which he adhered to so strongly in 1891, when he was struggling to attain the confidence of the Canadian people. I say my right hon. friend occupies a very invidious position in the light of the words which I have just quoted, when he declines or is unable to answer a question so pointedly put to him, a question so near the heart of this great question which affects so deeply the honour of this great Dominion. Along that line I might ask the right hon. gentleman another Mr. BOYCE.
question: will he deny that in 1891 he affirmed that if a minister accepted gifts of money without ascertaining himself and then making public the list of the subscribers thereto, he was aiming a blow at public morality? Can my right hon. friend answer that question? Will my right hon. friend deny that if the act of giving testimonials to ministers was done in. the open light of day, it would be the best safeguard that there could possibly be against any wrong taking place? I must confess that I never saw the right hon. gentleman so reluctant to answer questions in this House as he is to-day. I would ask him whether he did not affirm in this House in 1891 that the receiving of such testimonials without publicity was causing the name of Canada to become a byword and a reproach? The Prime Minister stated in May, 1910, that there was a list. An hon. friend near me suggests that I should go further and ask the right hon. gentleman whether he saw the list of subscribers to that testimonial? Mr. Speaker, I am speaking in all seriousness. My right hon. friend evaded my moderate question in this House on the 3rd of May, 1910, by saying that there was no name on the list which ought not properly to be read, and he pledged his responsibility as Prime Minister of this country to that effect. I ask him here and now whether he saw the list of names of persons who subscribed to that testimonial,, and with the utmost pleasure I will takei my seat to give my right hon. friend an opportunity to reply to that most potent question-Mr. Speaker, notwithstanding that I gave place to my right hon. friend, he still elects to maintain a silence which' in my humble judgment is anything bufi dignified. I will ask him one more question on this, most important matter: Was he not present and did he not see the testimonial presented to the hon. Minister of Finance, and did he not approve of it, applaud it, and at the time he approved of it had he seen the list of persons who subscribed to it? I ask the right hon. gentleman again whether he was not present when that testimonial was presented to the Finance Minister, whether he did not approve of it and applaud it, and whether he had not at the time a list of those who subscribed to it? Will he answer that question? He is silent, but if any significance is to be attached to the stand he took in 1891 and the charges he made against the Conservative party of that day in that connection, it is of the utmost importance now that we should have from him a full disclosure of all the facts. And I say that he is not upholding the dignity of the, country when he refuses to answer a question of such pith and moment. It is

a question, in the asking of which I am within my rights and privileges in this free parliament, and it is a question, in' refusing to answer which, the right hon. gentleman shows his autocratic contempt for the people and their representatives. In view of the right hon. gentleman's silence, may I again ask him now whether he is prepared to affirm that a cabinet minister may properly receive money from any source and refuse to make public the subscribers of that money, so as to satisfy public opinion that there is no wrong? I see the hopelessness of trying to get from the right hon. gentleman further information and must simply draw the only conclusion which can be drawn from his continued silence.
What is the position in which the right hon. gentieman and the subscribers to this fund have placed the Minister of Finance? In what position is the Minister of Finance after accepting, upon the assurance, no doubt, given him by the Prime Minister that it was all right, that nothing was too good for Fielding-what is the position in which the Finance Minister finds himself after accepting this gift, without seeing the list of those who gave it? What a commentary on the conduct of the Finance Minister must be the declaration of the right hon. gentleman made in 1891 as to what was right and proper in this connection? Can any one urge any good reason why the Prime Minister, in flat defiance of the principles! laid down by himself, should now refuse to publish the list? I am asking him in 1911 the very question which he himself hurled across the floor in 1891. My right hon. friend knew who subscribed to that testimonial to the Finance Minister and he must have pledged his responsibility, not only as a private citizen but as Prime Minister, that there was nothing improper in connection with it. Then, in the name of all that is fair and reasonable, why does he not make the list of subscribers public? How long is he going, to allow this condition of things to continue? How long is it going to be possible for newspapers all through the country, without fear of libel suits, to make statements reflecting on the honour and credit of ministers of the Crown? Why does he not remove the, aspersions that are being cast on himself and his colleagues? If there be no improper subscription, let him publish the list and raise even at this late hour the cloud which rests on the Minister of Finance and which must continue to rest on him so long as this information is withheld. The very evil at which the resolution of the right hon. the Prime Minister in 1891 was aimed is the one which is now being perpetrated by him. I am of the opinion that public men who serve in the capacity of ministers of the Crown should be adequately rewarded. They
sacrifice a great deal, they sacrifice their personal means and health, they give to their country all their ability, all their time and all their strength; and 1 say that when the Minister of Finance in 1905 introduced a measure to provide life pensions for Privy Councillors, he did the right thing. And I know of no valid reason which warranted the hori. gentleman repealing in 1906 the measure which he put through the House in 1905 and in thus subjecting cabinet ministers to embarrassements such as are now being experienced by the Minister of Finance. On the 17th Anril, 1905, the Finance Minister moved a Bill which went through its three leadings based upon this resolution:
That it is expedient that every member of the Privy Council, who has served as cabinet ministers and head of a department for a period of five consecutive years shall, upon retirement from the cabinet, be entitled to receive out of the consolidated revenue of Canada

Not out of personal subscriptions

If any person receiving an annuity hereunder becomes entitled to any salary in respect of any public office under the government of Canada, or to the additional sessional allowance provided for the leader of the opposition in the House of Commons, such salary or allowance shall be reduced by the amount of such annuity.
Sir, what was that Bill for? My hon. friend in moving that said that cabinet ministers were in the same position as judges, they had similar duties to perform, they were in the same dignified position and should be provided for to the same extent. That is a very rational and logical argument and one that calls for this question which I will address to all hon. gentlemen sitting on the government benches: What would they think of a judge occupying a seat on the bench receiving a testimonial from erstwhile clients or suiters, from litigious or lion-litigious persons who might at any date have suits before him? Would my hon. friend think it decent or proper that a judge of the High Court should receive such a testimonial of large sums of money? It would have been far better if the Minister of Finance had stuck to his bill of 1905 instead of receding from it in 1906 and saying that he was in favour of it, that he thought the principle was a sound one but was afraid of public opinion. I wonder if he is less afraid of public opinion now. This is what the Prime Minister said on that question on July 10, 1996:

Never before has there been a greater example on the part of any Canadian citizen of devotion to duty than the example shown for fourteen years while Minister of Finance by Hon. Mr. Fielding. During that fourteen years, he has served this country as well as any public man ever served any country. And, let me add. expressions of kindliness, of appreciation, of confidence, were just as common from Conservatives as they were from members of the Liberal party. And it may not be generally .known to members of this House or to the people of Canada that, time and again, on more than one occasion, Hon. Mr. Fielding, Minister of Finance, has been offered, and has refused, from private business institutions salaries far in advance of any he has ever received or any indemnity ever given him as Finance Minister of this Dominion.
As chairman of the Banking and Commerce Committee, during last session and the session before, when the committee was very busily engaged with the general insurance Act, 'in which members of both sides of the House took a deep interest, day after day, I noticed that Mr. Fielding, who was at my side while I presided over that committee, would call a messenger as the hour of adjournment approached, and send him for a lunch to be taken to Mr. Fielding's room. And, in place of spending an hour or an hour and a half as business men are in the habit of doing, in club or lunch-room, Mr. Fielding partook of his lunch while dictating letters or reading correspondence. It is a fact well known to every member of this House and to a great many business men of Canada at least, that Hon. Mr. Fielding has so devoted his time and thought and energy to the duties of his position and the interests of Canada, that he has paid not the slightest regard to his own business affairs, his own fortune, or the accumulation of any provision for himself or his family. I have heard members on both sides speak in the highest terms of Mr. Courtney, who was, until a few years ago, Deputy Finance Minister. Mr. Courtney is a man of experience, and a man of undoubted integrity, and, so far as he has any political leanings those leanings are to the Conservative party; he was appointed by a Conservative government. I happened to be walking one afternoon with Mr. Courtney some time after he had re-Mr. EDWARDS
signed his position as Deputy Minister of Finance. He spoke of Mr. Fielding. He said that Hon. Mr. Fielding came from Nova Scotia to accept the position of Finance Minister of Canada, a fresh vigorous, hearty young man, with hair as black as raven's wings; but, he said, that with these years of devotion to duty and to his country, his hair had become whitened. And he said: ' There is not a man in Canada, whatever may be his politics, who would dare to point a finger of suspicion at Hon. Mr. Fielding, Sir, we are all proud to know that that is true. The hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Foster), speaking last night, speaking, perhaps, jocosely,- said: ' If the people of Canada were foolish enough to continue in power much longer the government that now controls the affairs of the country.' Sir, if the Liberal party have been in power for fourteen years, and if, as I anticipate, they will be in power for fourteen years yet to come, it is largely because of two reasons, and of two personages. The first is the Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier). _ The people of this Dominion, the business men, the thinking men, of Canada, for fourteen years., have believed, as they believe today, that there is no other Canadian so well fitted to fill the position of Prime Minister as is the gentleman who now fills and adorns that position. And no less truly do the business men of Canada, whether they be Liberals or Conservatives, believe, as they have believed for the last fourteen years, that Canada has never had a Finance Minister equal in his devotion, in his integrity, in his ability, to Hon. W. S. Fielding. Sir, business men in Canada, even Conservatives, men whose every vote has been cast for the Conservative party, have hesitated to mark their ballots against this government, for the very fear that, some man other than Hon. W. S. Fielding might control the financial affairs of this country. And one of the strongest cards it has been possible to play for the Liberal government in any part of this country is to ask, ' If you vote Hon. W. 8. Fielding out of office as Finance Minister in Canada, whom do you think you are
voting in ?'	. , ,	,,
It would not have been Tight, it would not have been fair, it would scarcely have been honourable or honest,-for Hon. W. S. Fielding, when men who had no connection whatever with this government, not government oflicials, not government contractors, not men who had alliances in any way with the government, chose to Jire-sent him with a magnificent sum of money as an evidence of their esteem, of their confidence, of their approval of his longtime work for Canada-I say that when men of that class chose to present a money token to Hon. W. S. Fielding, it would not

have been right or honourable, having his family in view, for him to have refused that gift. Neither would it have been a nice thing for the gentlemen who proffered the gift to have had it refused in that way. The Hon. W. S. Fielding has given his whole life and has sacrificed his health in the service of this country ; he has refused financial positions yielding much greater revenue; and this he has done out of love for the country quite as much as any military general who has lost his life on his country's battlefields. And, Sir, when a man who has been of such great value to the country of which he is proud to be a citizen, is asked to accept a gift which has been proffered to him by his friends, I say it is not to the credit of this House that even one of its members should have been willing to make the charge which has been made to-day. Sir, I take up the morning ' Citizen ' of this city, a Conservative newspaper, and I read in it the following expression of opinion spoken by one of the clergymen of the city in his pulpit last Sunday morning:
Right of Parliament-Rev. J. W. H. Milne Condemns Actions of some Members.
