subtopic: TESTIMONIALS TO MINISTERS OF THE CROWN.
speechtext:
Milne, in his sermon Sunday in Glebe Presbyterian church, in referring to men being able to differ and yet remain friends, said:
Some men in politics can agree to differ. Some men can contend openly and honourably, yet withal retain no unkindly feeling. But even now and then there are men, even members of parliament, who are so venomous in their opposition to those who differ from them that they are ready to suggest or say anything that will leave a stain on the character of an opponent. There is something essentially villainous in the makeup of a man who, in order to gain his ends politically, will accept any story floating about and then ask a question, because privileged, with the object of destroying another who may be opposed to him. But worse still is it for any member of parliament, because shielded by four walls, to bring before the public the name of any man against whom he may have a grudge, on mere pretext of suspicion. Any man may have his name brought before the House by any member. He may be maligned by innuendos. He may, although innocent, have suspicion cast on his character, yet have no means of redress.
This may be called the right of parliament but it is not in harmony with the spirit of Christian civilization. No civilized community would tolerate the highwayman who would jump from an ambush and steal the purse of a respectable citizen and yet we permit political highwaymen, to stand up in the House and rob sincere, earnest citizens of their character. There must eventually be some means provided which will prevent such public outrages.
Sir, if I should make the application of that article which I should like, you would at once rule out my language as unparlia-88J
mentary. I am glad to believe that there is in this country perhaps only one representative of the press who would so demean himself as to have spread that garbled and false report through the length and breadth of Canada as to the contribution from W. R. Travers to the Fielding fund. And I think the hon. member who spoke this afternoon when he knew that a proper denial had been made of the story, ought at least to have been sufficiently manly to have made some reference to that denial. I hope, Sir, that, with more years of parliamentary experience, if by any chance or by any foolishness of the electorate the hon. gentleman is permitted to continue in this House, he will some day regret the action he has taken to-day, and will apologize, as I believe an apology is due, to the House, to his constituents, and to the particular member who was the object of his attack.

maintopic: SUPPLY-MR. J. A. MACDONALD AND RECIPROCITY.
subtopic: TESTIMONIALS TO MINISTERS OF THE CROWN.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I regard it as a subject of regret that any hon. member of this House should be ready to take up a false statement, started by some evil-minded person, and give it so much publicity. I am aware that it is the right of every hon. member to do so;.but with that right| there is a corresponding responsibility. In>
my judgment the man who circulates a>
false story is only a degree less guilty than the man who starts it originally. If an hon. member is to deal seriously and not flippantly with a question of this kind, he ought to be able to 'produce somei proof; he ought to be brave enough to make a charge and put behind it some kind of proof before he brings the matter before the House. My hon. friend from West Algoma (Mr. Boyce) has not had the courage to do anything of the kind.
As I acted as a humble member of the committee in charge of the testimonial question, I think it is due to the House and to the hon. Minister of Finance that I should say a few words. I will not, discuss the general subject of donations! tjQ cabinet ministers. My opinion is that this discussion is brought on, not for the, purpose of settling any general principle* but for the mere purpose of making an unpi'ovoked attack upon the character of the Minister of Finance. This is clearly understood on both sides of the House, and it is very well understood in the country. Now, Sir, I wish to assure the House as a member of that committee that the statement made in the press and repeated in this House by the hon. member for West Algoma on the 23rd day of this month, that Mr. W. R. Travers, the late manager of the Farmers' Bank, contributed $2,500 to the Fielding memorial, is false. Not one dollar of that memorial was contributed by Mr. Travers; not one

dollar of the memorial was contributed by the Farmers' Bank, or I may say by any other hank in Canada. I wish also to assure the House that the committee was scrupulously careful that no money should be accepted from contractors, from corporations, from banks or from any party having any dealings with the government. That was the understanding on which the memorial was started, and that understanding was very carefully carried out by every member of the committee. Every dollar of that memorial was clean money contributed by the personal friends and admirers of the Minister of Finance; and I am glad to repeat, what has already/ been said in the House, that some of those are to be found in the ranks of the Conservative party. I also desire to assure the House that the utmost secrecy Sjas maintained by the committee, and that the names of the contributors were not given to the Minister of Finance. I question if he knows to-day the name of a single man who contributed to the memorial.
The fact that after 30 years of faithful service devoted to his country, his closest friends felt that something of that kind was necessary is of itself sufficient proof of the integrity and honesty of the Minister of Finance, i cannot think that the Conservative party as a whole-and I feel sure that the Conservative party in this House -are not behind the hon. member for West Algoma (Mr. Boyce) in the attack he has made this afternoon upon the Minister of Finance. It is quite clear that the applause which met his remarks did not come from the front benches of the opposition. My hon. friend quoted some newspapers of the baser sort speaking for the Conservative party. Let me quote in my turn from the press, and I shall not now quote from the Liberal, but from the Conservative press. I want to be permitted to read an editorial which appeared in the Kingston ' Standard,' which, I am told, is one of the old time Conservative papers of Ontario. At one time, I believe it was the organ of the late Sir John Macdonald, and is one of the decent and respectable Tory papers in this country-and I am glad to say there are a number of them. It is not a scurrilous newspaper like the Toronto ' Mail and Empire ' and others I could mention. It is one of the good old fashioned, simon pure Tory papers which believes in British fair play, and I wish to be permitted to read the editorial. This is what the Kingston ' Standard ' says.
We cannot see how any political advantage is to be gained out of the statement put in circulation by sundry people and newspapers that W. R. Travers contributed $2,500 to the fund which made up the purse to the Hon. Mr. Fielding, Minister of Finance. In the first place, there seems no warrant or founda-Mr. SINCLAIR.
tion for the statement; and in the second place, it is one of those petty, miserable, nasty charges that usually do their originators more harm than good-and per contra, usually do more good than harm to the person or persons at whom they are directed. Fair play in politics is, it seems to us, as necessary as fair play in business-but this charge is not fair; it is merely contemptible, for we all know, and it was announced at the time, that Mr. Fielding has never been told, has not known and does not want to know who were the contributors to his fund.
For our own part we have felt that in respect to this gift to Mr. Fielding that it could not possibly make any difference to him in his official capacity or conduct. If he is honest-and we think he is-the gift would not make him dishonest. If he is dishonest the gift would not make him more so. But, however this he, one thing is certain, and .that is that no harm will come to him through innuendos and sneers that are not worthy any decent newspaper or any decent man.
It's a great thing to know how to play a game-even a political game-fairly.
That is the opinion of one of the respectable newspapers supporting the party of my hon. friend from West Algoma (Mr. Boyce). It would seem, Mr. Speaker, that in these days the good name of no public man is altogether safe, especially if he takes an active part in political warfare. The late Alexander Mackenzie is now universally regarded as having been a disinterested jpure-minded statesman. Honesty and integrity are admitted to have been his chief characteristics. If any one should happen to mention Mr. Mackenzie he would say of him: Well, there is an honest man. In the history of this country, Mr. Mackenzie is considered as the Sir Galahad of Canadian public life. Yet one has only to 'turn back to the newspapers and to 'Hansard ' of that day to find that the scavengers were busy trying to blacken his character. But, thank God, they failed, and the character of the Hon. Alexander Mackenzie stands to-day as an example and inspiration to young men of Canada. This attack of my hon. friend on the Minister of Finance, I regard as an analogous case. The Finance Minister had just returned from a successful mission to a foreign government. Everybody was glad, hon. gentlemen in this House generally on both sides were glad, to welcome him back and to see that his health was improved. The people of Canada, from Cape Breton to Victoria, were listening with interest to the message he brought back from Washington, and he brought back a proposed treaty which ought to earn for him the gratitude of every patriotic ;Canadian ; hut scarcely had he taken his seat in this House when he discovered that an hon. member of this House had been spending his time during his absence gathering up mud to throw at him. I want to say in closing to the scavengers outside this House-I am quite

well aware that if I were to call a member of this House a scavenger, I would be called to order-I want to say to the scavengers that their attempt to besmirch or blacken the character of the Hon. Mr. Fielding will fail. Mr. Fielding is too well known in Canada, and wherever he is known, he is respected, honoured and loved. His 15 years of faithful public service in his own native province have not been forgotten, and the 14 years during which he acted as the lieutenant of our great leader, and helped to shape the course and guide tile destiny of this country in the larger arena will always tbe one of the brightest chapters in the history of Canada. Let me tell you, Sir, that the reputation and the good faith of the Minister of Finance is one of the most precious possessions of the Canadian people. Any one who attempts to besmirch or blacken that good fame will earn the contempt from all decent Canadians that his conduct deserves. Let the scavengers throw mud if they will, it will not stick. It -did not stick to Mr. Mackenzie, and it will not stick to Mr. Fielding.
At six o'clock, House took recess.
After Recess.
House resumed at eight o'clock.

maintopic: SUPPLY-MR. J. A. MACDONALD AND RECIPROCITY.
subtopic: TESTIMONIALS TO MINISTERS OF THE CROWN.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I shall slightly vary the trend of my remarks this evening owing to the attitude assumed by hon. gentlemen opposite. I had intended to speak, as far as possible, in a purely judicial way. I shall endeavour to do so' still, but I shall bring into discussion several matters that I would have been disposed to leave out had not supporters of the government assumed such an extraordinary attitude in reference to this motion. We have reached a very unfortunate pass in Canadian affairs if a member of this House, feeling it to be his duty to do so, as it would have been the duty of many other members of this House, may not venture to bring to your attention and to the attention of the House and of the country the extraordinarv circumstances that present themselves in connection with the gift of about $120,000 to a minister of the Crown. I am quite prepared to join with anv lion, gentleman on the other side of the House in paying tribute where it is necessary, not a pecuniary tribute, but a meed of praise to any minister of the Crown who honourably and faithfully discharges his duties. I am not prepared to join with the hon. member for South Grey (Mr. Miller) and the hon. member for Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair) who imagine that _ they should seize a circumstance that certainly reflects no credit upon the government or the Finance Minister as the occasion for fulsome and undeserved laudations such as we have had this afternoon. I have not understood that this side of the House launched any attack upon the Minister of Finance. I did not understand until the hon. member for Guysborough spoke that there was any mud-slinging. I have understood that the member for West Algoma thought it necessary, in view of circumstances that have transpired, to refer again in this House to the language which was so enthusiastically lauded by the First Minister in 1891, and from which unfortunately the ministers have signally and purposely departed. But in referring to that principle no attack has been made upon the Minister of Finance. Circumstances have arisen in connection with a gift to the Finance Minister, which having regard to the declarations of all parties in 1891, call upon the government at the earliest possible moment to make a full and fair disclosure of the persons who contributed to that testimonial. If there is an attack at all it is an attack	upon the
First Minister, certainly there is none upon the Minister of Finance. But I am prepared to say from my place in the House that I distinctly attack the position taken by the First Minister, for when I find an hon. gentleman like the First Minister declaring so emphatically in 1891 the principle and the only principle upon which a public testimonial can be made to a minister of the Crown and then find him in 1909 and 1910 distinctly going back on every statement he made on that occasion, I think it is time to call the attention of the House and of the public to the attitude of the First Minister. It is sometimes said among lawyers that in a certain class o<f cases the most unwise thing to do is to put your own client in the box and there has been no exception to that rule this afternoon, for whereas until I heard the Minister of Finance, I was prepared to believe that should the list be brought down it might establish that there were no improper contributions, I am not now prepared to take that attitude:	I thought that we were vindicating
the honour of the House by asking for the production of this document. I hoped it would show that the people had not been deceived and that contributions had not been made which ought not to have been made. I had hoped that the government would have vindicated their position by bringing down a statement of the names of the contributors and have shown that there was not one improper contribution upon that list. Why don't they do it as the right hon. gentleman said in 1891? Why don't they do it? Because they dare not do it. I challenge the First Minister now, after all that has been hurled from that side of the House, I challenge him again to get up in the House and implement the statements he made in 1891,

and say that for once he will redeem a pledge and a promise, and lay upon the table of the?House the statement that we are entitled to; and I will then join with him, or any other member of the House, in paying any reasonable measure of tribute to the Minister of Finance.
But the Finance Minister made a peculiar statement. He says, I was approached on one occasion many years ago, a gentleman proposed to make me a testimonial, and I absolutely refused. He was not tempted on that occasion. But they came again. Who were they? It would be very interesting to the people of this country to know. On that occasion the hon. gentleman parleyed, hg_hesitated, and to hesitate in a case of that kind is to be lost. He parleyed; his better judgment told him, as he said this afternoon, that the thing could not consistently be done. He says he felt that the probability was that if that subscription list was put in vogue, names would occur on it which ought not to be there, and ithere would be a political scandal. Therefore, tempted as he was- and I do not blame him for being tempted -he resisted their blandishments 'and their suggestions, and they went away. But the tempter came again, in, I think, a more unholy guise than before, came in the person of a gentleman that I will mention presently. I am no seer, but I think I can put my band upon that gentleman- not in this chamber ; but I think I can point him out, and I will point him out through the ' Globe ' newspaper presently. This gentleman came in a more tempting guise and said: We want to get up a testimonial-thoroughly disinterested, not one of the subscribers should derive anv benefit from the government, purely voluntary. Even if we are not disinterested, it is no matter, because we will never never fell who we are. And the minister listened to the voice of the tempter, and he fell; and Mr. Speaker, it was a great fall in the public life of Canada, it was a very unfortunate circumstance in the history of this country, it is something that will take us some time to wipe away. What does the minister tell us? He tells us that he made a bargain. Did you ever hear Mr. Speaker, the like before? He says: We made a hard and fast bargain, then and there, that this would be an absolute and inviolate secret for all time to come; we made a bargain behind the backs of the people whose servants we are. That is what the Minister of Finance tells us. He says: This gentleman bound himself that these names would never be divulged, and I bound myself that I wouid put mv head in the sand like an ostrich, and that I would never look to find out who these men were; and that in the meantime 1 Mr. LENNOX.
would go on as before, as if it had never happened, and administer the affairs of the Dominion of Canada, conscious though I might be, he says, that perhaps a lot of that money came from an unholy source, but I would not know it. So, he says, I made the bargain. I say, Mr. Speaker, that a more infamous bargain than that by which the Finance Minister pledged himself, to use the language of the First Minister, to be ' deaf and dumb, and blind ' for all time, was never made in the Dominion of Canada.
And was the. minister perfectly innocent in the matter ? I came here this afternoon prepared to say that in the career of the Minister of Finance, he had never put his hands into the treasury to enrich himself, that I would be in complete sympathy with him if he received private contributions from private friends, publicly made, in the face of day, before the people of Canada, and I would be glad if he got it, because I recognize that through no fault of his, perhaps, he needed it, and it was no reproach to him that he needed it. But today I have heard hon. gentlemen going out of their way to sling mud at this side of the House, and to laud the Minister of Finance as if, not only was he personally honest up to that time, but as if he were a paragon of political honesty, and an example to the people. I am not quite prepared to go that far, I recollect that in the history of this broad Dominion, where rampant extravagance has prevailed for the last twelve or fourteen years, where worse than extravagance has been witnessed in every part of the Dominion, there has been no member of parliament who has been less careful as to the manner in which he would hold his party in power, no member of this House who has Seen more reckless as to how the public money was being expended for the purpose of bringing grist to their own mill, than the Finance Minister of Canada. Whilst I am prepared to certify to his personal honesty up to this time, I am not able to close my eyes to the fact-which I would not have mentioned, but for the line the debate has taken that there has been no instance in the history of Canada, black as it is as regards the debauching of constituencies, so black as the case of the very constituency which is represented by the Minister of Finance.
Now was the Minister of Finance perfectly innocent in this infamous bargain? The fact that it was a secret bargain is a bad feature, the fact that it is kept secret is a presumption of guilt, and a very-strong one, when persisted in as we find here. But I venture to say, Mr. Speaker, that we have here the most cogent evidence that this bargain, made by the Minister of Finance, as he tells us, with those gentle-

men in ithe guise of friends, was not a fair and bona fide bargain. In other words-the Minister of Finance did not act in perfect good faith when he made that bargain, because he tells us, this mysterious gentleman told me that ' I would never be told who the contributors were.' So far so good. I agree to that, but, he says, before I let him go from me, I asked him for one concession. I said: I may retire from public life, and I might like to know before I die as to who they were who benefited me; will you grant this request that whilst it shall be inviolably concealed so long as it may Be a source of temptation to me to do wrong, it will be divulged to me after I retire from public life? Will the right hon. Prime Minister tell the House, if it was a perfectly legitimate transaction on the part of the Finance Minister and if it was bona fide intended that no gentleman was to contribute to this testimonial who could, in any way come in contact with the minister in his public office, how could there be any difference in the situation after he had retired from office from his situation while he remained in office ? So, in moderate language, I hope, but impelled by a sense of duty as a public man, I charge that the Finance Minister in the statement he made this afternoon, proved conclusively and incontestably that he had an inkling into that transaction and into the nature of it before he parted from the mysterious friend who beguiled him on that occasion.
Well, who was this truly benevolent personage, this truly good iman, who came to him and made this bargain ? It was not the hon. member for South Grey (Mr. Miller), it was not the chairman of the Banking and Commerce Committee. It was not he because he is not a big enough man for the position. It was a bigger man than that. If I have said that the gentleman of racecourse fame was not big enough for that situation I need not say that the member for Guysborough would not fill the bill. It was not he who came. Well then, who was it? Was it a gentleman by the name of Jaffray? I think we have pretty strong and conclusive evidence that it was. Let me recall to the House the description by the Minister of Finance of the gentleman who came here and you will see at once that it will not apply to the hon. member for South Grey or the hon. member for Guysborough. He says that he was a man occupying a very important position, a very distinguished gentleman, a man high up in social circles and so on in Canada, a man of irreproachable character and a man of the highest sense of honour. I wish we had him on file here just to examine him. When I got that picture I said to myself that I did not think there was anybody
who could fill the bill except Jaffray, that gentleman of immaculate purity, that white-robed angel, slightly sprinkled with coal dusit, who had performed certain injudicious, but very profitable pilgrimages into the Orowsnest Pass. But why did I think that it was Senator Jaffray ?

speechtext: He was one of them.

speechtext: He was one of them and a gentleman by the name of P. C. Larkin was another, and another of the beautiful quartette as far as is disclosed, was the hon. member for South Grey, the Under Secretary, if I may call him that, of the Minister of Finance, the chairman of the Banking Committee and a gentleman who can always whisper into the ear of the Minister of Finance, and tell him what he will; this man ought to go; this man ought to stay, and you can imagine what a valuable character he will be when the great Banking Act comes up for investigation at a very early date. I will have a word to say about the hon. member for South Grey, not because of his position, but because of his connection with this matter, later on.

maintopic: SUPPLY-MR. J. A. MACDONALD AND RECIPROCITY.
subtopic: TESTIMONIALS TO MINISTERS OF THE CROWN.
speechtext: And Larkin.

maintopic: SUPPLY-MR. J. A. MACDONALD AND RECIPROCITY.
subtopic: TESTIMONIALS TO MINISTERS OF THE CROWN.
speechtext:
Larkin is a gentleman who is-oh, he is a man of means-a man of ways and means. Well now, a certain newspaper that can sling mud almost as well as we can on this side of the House, as described by the hon. member for Guysborough, was attacking the member who introduced this resolution in its editorial columns on the 25th of January last. This is the ' Globe ' and it speaks of ' The detractors of Mr. Fielding.' As soon as it is asked to have a resolution passed affirming the attitude of these gentlemen, trying to re-establish them in their faith of 1891, the ' Globe ' takeis up t,he cudgels and attacks us as ' the detractors of Mr. Fielding.' In referring to what the hon. member for Algoma had given notice of, it says:
The whole fantastic fabric is founded on falsehood from beginning to end. Had Travers contributed $2,500 or any other sum to the testimonial, Mr. Fielding would never have known of it,

Mr. Fielding never would have known of it. That is rather a significant statement. We have this fact set out by the organ of the Grit party, the first organ of the Grit party in this country, that even Travers or any other criminal, had contributed to the testimonial Mr. Fielding would never have known of it ffnd innocently would have been enjoying the secret fruits of dishonesty.
-for to this day he has not seen or in any other way been informed of the names of the contributors so careful were those who arranged the testimonial to make sure that no

contributions would be given because of a lively sense of favours to come.
These gentlemen appreciate the situation, at all events.
Senator Jaffray

That is the gentleman in disguise who came to the Finance Minister

-and Mr. P. C. Larkin, who obtained the Toronto subscriptions,

And this with Montreal is the big end of it, with the smaller fry here in the House of Commons.
-desire it to be known that neither directly nor indirectly from Mr. Travers or any one on his behalf or on behalf of the farmers' Bank was any subscription received nor' was any subscription asked for or tendered.
Am I not right in assuming that the chief engineers of this whole affair were Jaffray and Larkin? Who is Mr. Jaffray and does he come within the limits of the definition laid down by the Liberals in 1891, by that great and good man, Sir Richard Cartwright, and by that almost equally immaculate gentleman, the right hon. First Minister who leads this House? Is Jaffray a contractor with the government or not?

maintopic: SUPPLY-MR. J. A. MACDONALD AND RECIPROCITY.
subtopic: TESTIMONIALS TO MINISTERS OF THE CROWN.
speechtext: Is Larkin?

maintopic: SUPPLY-MR. J. A. MACDONALD AND RECIPROCITY.
subtopic: TESTIMONIALS TO MINISTERS OF THE CROWN.
speechtext:
Is Larkin a contractor with the government or not? We know of Jaffray's connection with the * Globe ' and we know that the ' Globe ' has a better thing than this testimonial. Why not, when the ' Globe ' is annually in receipt of a tidy little sum from this government, part of it earned and a great deal of it not earned except by fulsome laudations and dishonest statements, of about $8,000 on the average So that this thing is coming fairly well home.
Before I go on, let me say, I am reminded that P. C. Larkin is not the contractor, but a tea man. And the tea men are getting a pretty nice tea party in connection with the transcontinental at the present time.
Now let me call attention to the attitude, which should be assumed by the government of Canada to contributions such as those under discussion, an attitude much loftier than is called for by the resoJ lution moved by my hon. friend from Algoma (Mr. Boyce). Hon. gentlemen will recall the incident in the life of Mr. Pitt. In 1789, when King George III. was found to be incapable of carrying on affairs of state, it was necessary to appoint a regent. I will read from Mr. Stanhope's work a short quotation which will show how this affected Mr. Pitt's fortunes. On three several occasions parties approached Mr. Pitt-his circumstances being of extreme difficulty-to give him the means of living-very like the Finance Minister in Mr. LENNOX.
that particular, but very much unlike the Finance Minister, in that Mr. Pitt declined on all three occasions; and different in this respect also, that while, when the first offer uras made to him Mr. Pitt was about to retire from public life, when the second proposal was made he had actually retired from public life, but yet, having regard to the fact that he might at some future time( re-enter public life (though it was pointed out to him that the, funds collected would be paid into a bank and he would never know the name of any contributor) he answered that he would never be able to meet any body without feeling that it might be one to whom he was indebted and declined. This is Mr. Stanhope's account of the situation:
By these votes of the Commons and the Lords the ground was cleared for Pitt's proposal with respect to the Regency Bill, a proposal hitherto kept secret, and indeed not yet fully matured. But during the interval he received a most signal token of the public esteem and approbation.
It was well known by the public that Pitt would not be continued one hour in office by the Regent. It was known that he had already taken measures for returning to his first profession. It was also known, perhaps, that his neglect of his private affairs had involved him in some debts, which he trusted to discharge by an industrious application of his talents at the bar. At this very time, however, there was held, by public advertisement, a meeting

his left hand know what his right hand was doing, and never give >a whisper to the Minister of Finance when he wanted recognition as a senator later on? The hon. member for Guysborough is peculiar too. He asks why the hon. member for West Algoma had not the courage to move a resolution? Where has the hon. gentleman been sleeping? Why the hon. member for West Algoma did move a resolution, and he did exactly what the friends of the hon. member for Guysborough did in 1891. It is in really trying to reinstate them in the faith they proclaimed then that we are moving this afternoon. But they will not be reinstated; they have had a. bad career in the meantime. Then he speaks of scavengers. He appears to be sensitive as to that, and I suppose it is hard, for he has been omitted from the list.
Now, what does this all mean? Mr. Jaf-fray and Mr. Larkin in Toronto, and the right hand man of the Minister of Finance, and the aspirant for a senatorship in the House of Commons-this combination of four handling 'this list, which is to be known to anybody they like to tell it to, but is not to be known to the people of Canada. It means this, that we, forsooth, are to take the statement of these gentlemen as to who was not on the list, but we are not to get a whisper as to who were on the list. It is not who was not on the list that we are after, and that the people are asking, and that they have a right to know, but who was on the list ; and they can judge for themselves whether they are proper contributors or not. It looks to me as if it were a general concerted scheme-the. hon. member for Guysborough to represent the maritime provinces, the hon. member for South Grey to represent the province of Ontario, Jaf-fray and company to represent the big financial city of Toronto, somebody not yet divulged-and he will not be divulged after what I have said-to represent Montreal, and somebody from the west-a general levy from God knows whom, because they will not tell us.
Now, I will refer briefly to the attitude of the present First Minister, and the Liberal party in 1891, and I will try to make it clear to the House and the country that the right hon. gentleman, in putting up these gentlemen to oppose this resolution, is taking back every statement he made in 1891 as to the proper conduct of members of the Crown in a situation of the kind. First, we have his first lieutenant, Sir Richard Cartwright, that gentleman whose soul was plunged in misery if anything crooked was done unless he had a hand in it himself. That gentleman, actuated by a sincere and holy desire in 1891, just after the death of Sir John Macdonald, the man who gave him so many and so well deserved thrashings in his lifetime, moved this Mr. LENNOX.
resolution in an effort to throw' mud upon the memory of that great statesman. Although I do not believe all that Sir Richard Cartwright said at all times, I think it quite fair to take him at his word on this occasion. Referring to Sir John Macdonald's need-and he made a few complimentary remarks to make it a little more stinging as he went along. He said;
Under these circumstances, if ever, it was quite justifiable for the hon. gentleman's personal friends and admirers to have contributed for the purpose of relieving his family from any danger of want, and had two or three very obvious and very reasonable precautions been taken, no blame could have been attached to the parties who -were concerned in getting up the testimonial.
That is not as high a code of morality as they have in Britain. According to the British code, a gentleman in public life, or likely to be again connected with public life should not take gifts at all; and I am prepared myself to subscribe to that doctrine although that is not the gist of the resolution this afternoon. But the hon. gentleman proceeded:
Unfortunately these precautions were not taken, unfortunately publicity was not given, as I have always said publicity should be given, to the names of those who subscribed.
What was the gist of this statement of Sir Richard Cartwright in 1891:	It was
that the only thing which could make the transaction defensible, was publicity, not merely publicity of the fact that there was a testimonial, but of the names of those who . subscribed. And the right hon. gentleman (Sir Wilfrid Laurier), who sits here and would not speak this afternoon, was the gentleman who congratulated Sir Richard Cartwright very warmly on the excellent speech he had made, and who subsequently was elated over the signal victory the opposition then won in having had this resolution, which we again propose this afternoon, voted unanimously by the Conservatives. Then Sir Richard goes on:
Still more unfortunately precautions were not taken to see that subscriptions to that fund were not accepted, save from sources from which they could honourably he accepted.
The hon. gentleman proceeds to make further observations which are still more, pertinent. I ask you, Mr. Speaker, to pay particular heed to these expressions and apply them to the facts now under discussion.
I have observed, Sir, that some of the hou. gentleman's apologists have undertaken to mitigate the error or the crime, call it what yon will, which was committed by the reception of that testimonial, under the circumstances, by the plea, which I think was also advanced in the other case, that the hon.

gentleman did not know who had subscribed to his testimonial. Such a plea

And that is the plea advanced toy; the Minister of Finance this afternoon, and which the Prime Minister advanced a few months ago.
-such a plea, in my judgment, is a direct aggravation of the offence. A public minister has no right whatever to allow any gift to be made to him unless it is done publicly and unless he knows from what source it proceeds; and, Sir, I would say this, that if a minister of the Crown tells me that he has accepted a gift, not knowing and not choosing to know from whom it proceeded, so far from regarding such a plea as a mitigation, I say that such a plea raises a presumption of guilt.
How does that meet the case to-night ?
It was his duty to find out; it was his duty to see that not one penny went into his pockets or into his coffers unless it came from such sources that he could honourably and fairly receive it.
Did the rigiht hon. the Prime Minister adopt that view when he congratulated Sir Richard Cartwright some 20 years ago on the speech he then made in this House ? If he did, and he did, how can he justify to the people, how can he justify to his own conscience, his own conduct in swallowing himself as he is doing on this occasion. Well, Mr. Speaker, Sir Richard Cartwright is now a kind of back number, and we will take the utterances of the Prime Minister himself, and ask him to apply them to the circumstances of to-day. Then if he -can get up and tell us that he can honourably discharge his duties and act consistently with the statement he then made, and yet say that the public are not entitled to know who were the subscribers to this fund, he is performing an acrobatic feat in- morals and politics, which I did not think even he was capable of. The right hon. gentleman then said:-
The Minister of Justice said a moment ago, in referring to the testimonial offered to the honourable Minister of Public Works, the member for Three Rivers, that that hon. gentleman did not know who were the subscribers. Sir,

You can imagine the dramatic attitude and pose of the right hon. gentleman as he said these words:-
-Sir, if he did not know, why did be not look at the list

I ask the right hon. gentleman why the Finance Minister, if he did not know who were the subscribers, * why he did not look at the list '? If the Finance Minister does not know, why does he not? It is because, before one dollar was subscribed to that fund, he entered into this
utterly indefensible bargain as he has said this afternoon, that the whole thing should be done in a hole and corner behind the backs of the people of Canada and that the people should never know, because it might happen that there were subscribers to that testimonial whose names it would not be safe to make public or to disclose to the hon. gentleman himself even after he had retired from public life. But let me go on to quote what the right hon. gentleman then said:-
If the hon. gentleman did not know, it was because he chose to remain ignorant of the names on the list, and if he chose to be ignorant, is it not because his moral sense told -him that he might there find names of persons giving contributions which should not be accepted at all. Is it not simply because his conscience told him that if he were to look at that list he would find there the names of men who every day were suppliants in his office for favours.
Has the right hon. gentleman's moral sense completely died out? Where is it to-night? Will the moral sense of the government permit them to longer continue this infamy, because it is an infamy to hide from the people of Canada these transactions in which they are fnost vitally interested. I ask the First- Minister if it is not simply because his conscience told him that if he were to look at that list he would find there the names of men who are every day suppliants in his office for favours. How is it to-night? Is it not true and does the First Minister not know it that if they were to look at that list they would find there hordes of. men, the majority of them men who, in a political sense, are from day to day suppliants in the office of the Minister of Finance for favours at the hands of the government? The hon. gentleman pronounced judgment upon it himself and I think we will leave it with that judgment. The right hon. gentleman says, summing it all up, that is the reason, the sense of conscience, the knowledge that they would be condemned in 1891 was the reason that they would not look at the list, and he says of the dead minister, that greatest statesman Canada has ever had, Sir John A. Macdonald, that was the reason that they would not look at the list. That is the reason why the Minister of Public Works did not choose to look at that list. And now that is not tihe reason why do they choose to be blind in the matter ? I call upon hon. gentlemen opposite to tell what is the reason if there can be any good reason for it. The right hon. gentleman has for the time being the matter in his hands. He ran refuse to give us this list. If it is a list such as they want us to understand it is, it will redound to the glory and to the honour of the Minister of Finance. If it is an honest list, if it is a list of persons who have the right to contribute, then the fair

name of the Minister of Finance will be vindicated above all question. Is that not a matter of some importance in the interests of Canada? Is that not a matter that ought to commend itself to the First Minister? Is that not a matter which he should grasp with eagerness ? Is it not a reasonable request on behalf of the people of Canada which the opposition are making to-nicnt? If it is not, will the First Minister tell us vhy it is not? I tell the First Minister that when he calls on his followers to vote down this resolution, as he is evidently prepared to do, he is putting a blacker mark upon his record than he has ever put there before, that there' is no more complete and utter denial of a former attitude taken by any political party in this country that the right-about-face of the government and their supporters if they vote down this resolution. Politically speaking I care not at all which it done, Nationally speaking I would be glad indeed if that list were produced, and if it appeared that there was not one name upon, it that ought not to be there, but I despair, after what I heard this afternoon, that this would be the case, for surelv there could be no good reason, there can be and there is no honest reason for refusing it unless it be that the right hon. gentleman and his followers know that they dare not produce if.

speechtext:
Do these gentlemen who laugh know the circumstances under which that motion of 1891 was made? When Sir Richard Cartwright made his motion in 1891, a Conservative paper in the city of Montreal, a paper which generally supported the administration, had been writing a series of articles appearing day after day, week after week, and month after month, which were republished afterwards in pamphlet form, and in which a charge was made against Sir Hector Langevin, that he had accepted a gift to which public contractors had contributed. Sir, that was the case in 1891. 1 stated last year when this matter came before the House that I did not care to speak of the dead, I did not care to repeat what I said in 1891 in the presence of Sir Hector Langevin, I did not care to read before the House what I then read in the House in the presence of Sir Hector Langevin.
But, Sir, I stated then, and I have to repeat again, that the occasion of the motion made by Sir Richard Cartwright was the fact that it was publicly stated, not in the press of the opponents of Sir Hector Langevin, but in the press of himself and his own friends, that public contractors had contributed to the fund which he had accepted. That was the reason why Sir Richard Cart-wright moved the motion which he did, and which I shall quote at

the present time. Sir Richard Cartwright in the face of that statement which was current, which was repeated day after day, that contributions had been made by contractors, moved this resolution:-
That the acceptance of gifts or testimonials of any kind on the part of ministers of the Crown or of any members of their families from contractors, government officials or other persons having pecuniary relations with the government, is entirely opposed to sound principles of administration and is calculated to bring parliamentary government into contempt; and that the example thus given tends to corrupt and demoralize the officials serving under ministers who have accepted or permitted the acceptance of gifts or testimonials as aforesaid.
Nobody will take exception to this. Everybody will admit that it would be disruptive of all public morals if contractors, government officials, or persons having pecuniary relations with the government should contribute to a fund for a minister. That was affirmed, it was not denied by anybody, it was an obvious truth. That motion was accepted and has ever since been the law of this parliament. It is recorded in our journals that such should be the law which should govern all men having anything to do with the public affairs of this country. I went further upon that occasion, and I stated that, in view of the circumstances, in my humble judgment, all such contributions should he made public.
Now, Sir, were those view's accepted on that occasion by the over-scrupulous gentlemen who now compose the Conservative party? When I stated that in my humble judgment the motion merely was not sufficient but that there should be another one to implement the first and to say that in order to make doubly sure in this case, especially in the case of Sir Hector Lange-vin, there should be publicity given to these proceedings, was the resolution adopted? Was it made the law of parliament as it was decided that the other motion should be the law of parliament? Not at all. My views, I was told this afternoon, were then thundered forth on the other side of the House, but if they were thundered forth they met with no response at all from the other side of the House and it has taken them twenty years to find out that there was some merit in them. But, if the motion and my views which I uttered and which I gave in all sincerity on that occasion had been received by the then government of the day they would have been made the law of parliament, as the motion of Sir Richard Cartwright was, and everybody would have been guided by that law. Now that has been the history of this question in so far as the previous proceedings of the House are concerned.

My hon. friend the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) was approached a year ago, and everybody knows that the Minister of Finance is not a wealthy man. His friends knew that he was a poor man. His friends knew that he was in the condition of Wm. Pitt, that he was still more in the condition of Sir John Macdonald, having a wife and children dependent upon him. My hon. friend the Minister of Finance w'as approached and he stated that he would agree to such a testimonial provided it was well understood that the lines laid down by the resolution of this House were strictly adhered to and that nobody would be permitted to contribute to the fund who was a public contractor, who was a government official, or any other person having pecuniary relations with the government. To anybody who knows the Minister of Finance, nay, I would say, is anybody on that side of the House who knows the Minister of Finance, not convinced that no matter how extremely dire might be the necessity of my friend and colleague he would not accept a dollar or a cent from that class of people who are mentioned in the motion? Is there a man on this side of the House, is there a man in this country, is there a man who has ever had anything to do with the man who is known as W. 8. Fielding, who is not fully aware that his conscience would not permit him under such circumstances to do anything which would he at all contrary to his sense of honour. Sir, I believe I cam say that even on that side of the House, there is not a man who would not be ready to say, and to say now, that the Minister of Finance is incapable of any mean action of whatever kind it may be. The Minister of Finance stipulated first that he would accept this testimonial if it were well understood that the men who would he at the head of the committee would not accept a dollar from any man who w'as a public contractor, a government official or who had any pecuniary transactions with the government. Every man has his own sense of honour, every man is the guardian of his own honour and if my hon. friend the Minister of Finance is characterized by any qualities-and he has many qualities to characterize him-he is mainly characterized by his sense of honesty, by his most delicate sense of honour. My hon. friend said he would not want to know those who had contributed to him so that, walking at out, whether it was in public or private life, he wanted to be absolutely unaware of the unknown friends who had come to his rescue under the circumstances in which he was.
Now, Sir, I was sorry to hear my hon. friend from South Simcoe (Mr. Lennox) a moment ago, deprecating this attitude of the Minister of Finance. I may say again to my hon. friend what I told him a mo-

ment ago, that in his calmer moments, when, to-morrow, having forgotten the sense of excitement under which he was provoked to speak, he reads his own words, he will be sorry for one of the aspersions, the insinuation, which he made against the character of the Minister of Finance. The minister was blamed by my hon. friend because he did not want to know the names of those who had contributed to that fund. He relied upon the honour of the men who had been charged by that committee to levy this fund to ask no government contractor, no government official,.no man having any pecuniary relations with the government to contribute anything to it. He relied that they would comply with that condition, and he stipulated that even the names of those unknown friends who were to assist him should not then be made known to him. My hon. friend blamed the Minister of Finance for this. Well, Sir, I leave it to him whether the Minister of Finance is not right. Perhaps another man would have said : No, I prefer to have them known. But, after all, if the Minister of Finance preferred under such circumstances, that he should not even know those to whom he might be grateful, he consulted his conscience, he consulted his honour; and the man does not live who can find fault with him for the decision he came to. Men there may be on the other side of the House, men there may be on this side of the House, who, putting aside all political proclivities and consulting only their higher sense of public honour and public morality, may differ upon that point with the Minister of Finance and may say that that hon. gentleman would have done better had he scrutinized that list himself. But he preferred to take the course he did; and I say that this is a question which, whether solved one way or whether solved another way, can reflect no dishonour upon the Minister of Finance. For my part, I said, speaking under different circumstances it is true

My words are cheered by hon. gentlemen opposite, in this year 1911; but similar words of mine gained no such response when I uttered them in 1891. But I have to say, the Minister of Finance did not violate the law of parliament as laid down in 1891; he did not violate any code of honour, nor any principle of honesty. He acted frankly and above board. And to-day he gave his version of the matter like a man. If any conclusion
is to be drawn from the words of the Minister of Finance, uttered under great provocation to-day on the floor of this House, it is not the conclusion urged by my hon. friend from Simcoe (Mr. Lennox); but tomorrow the name of W. S. Fielding will be dearer to the people than it is at the present time. Say what you will, do what you may, the man is not living who can breathe suspicion upon the character of my hon. friend the Minister of Finance, Hon. W. S. Fielding.
I have stated that upon these matters a difference of judgment is always possible. But I am asked: How are we going to judge ? In 1891, there was not only a suspicion against Sir Hector Langevin, there was an open charge, as I said a moment ago, day after day, and week after week these charges appeared in the press and they were published in pamphlet form under the title ' Le Metier de Ministre.' It was openly charged against Sir Hector Langevin that he had accepted contributions from contractors, that at the very moment when he -was sitting in the House he had the money of contractors in his pocket. Is there to-day a suspicion that Mr. Fielding has a cent of public money in his pocket? No, Sir, in this country public men are liable to find charges made against them;-I do not complain of that, it is part of the game. We are liable to be accused, to be traduced; every man who takes his seat in this House, must be prepared for that. But there are, after all, certain things, however we may differ, which, in our heart of hearts, we know to be true. And there is not a man on that side of the House, as there is not a man on this side, but knows that my hon. friend the Minister of Finance is absolutely incapable of a dishonest, a low, a mean action, word or thought.
I do not find fault with the hon. member for West Algoma for bringing this question forward again; the only fault I have to find with him is, because of the manner in which he has brought it forward. He brings it forward in such a form that an amendment would be out of order, forcing us on this side of the House either to adopt it entire, or vote it down entire. In his speech, my hon. friend took me to task again and again. He wanted me to speak when I did not feel inclined to speak; he wanted me to do his bidding, when I had no intention of doing his bidding. He must not find fault if I did not respond as he wished me to do; it is my privilege as a man, to speak and act as and when I wish. I do not find fault with the hon. gentleman's speech, but I repeat, that I do find fault with the manner in which he introduced the resolution.

I have answered that already. When Sir Richard Cartwright moved his motion, if I remember well, it was in the month of July or August, and at a time when parliament had been in session for five months or so. At that time every day was a government day, and Sir Richard Cartwright had no other method of bringing the question forward than that which he adopted. My hon. friend (Mr. Boyce), is not in that position. He could have moved his motion on Monday, on Wednesday, and could have moved it at a time when we might have amended it. But I will go further with my hon. friend. When I came into this House to-day, I was disposed to say that to the first part of the resolution there was no objection whatever; we have voted it before, and would be ready to vote it again; but as to the second part of the resolution, I would have been prepared to ask the hon. gentleman to modify it so as to make it more acceptable than it is. For the hon. gentleman must realize, as the House will realize, that it is couched in offensive language. The first part of the resolution reads as follows:-
That the acceptance of gifts or testimonials of any kind on the part of ministers of the Crown or of any members of their families from contractors, government officials or other persons having pecuniary relations with the government, is entirely opposed to sound principles of administration, and is calculated to bring parliamentary government into contempt, and that the example thns given tends to corrupt and demoralize the officials serving under ministers who have accepted or permitted the acceptance of gifts or testimonials as aforesaid.
I may say to my hon. friend that there was no necessity for his introducing this part of the resolution at all, for it is part of the law of this parliament already. It has been on our Journals for 20 years. Therefore there is no necessity for affirming it now. My hon. friend is not so clever that we cannot see through him: he introduces this part in order to take the other part, which I shall now read:
That in order to maintain this principle the source of any gifts of money to ministers of the Crown ought not to he surrounded with secrecy, and that an authentic statement of the donors should be made public.
