BORDEN (Halifax i Mr. Speaker, I have seen the right hon. gentleman in pretty tight places on many occasions, but I have never seen him struggle so hard and accomplish so little as he has done to-night, I am perfectly confident that that is his own sensation and conviction at this moment. I will come a little later on to some of the arguments-I suppose it is necessary, in a parliamentary point of view, to dignify them by that name-and deal with them in detail. For the moment I want to point out to the House that the two strong points which the right hon. gentleman has made are these: first, that Sir Richard Cartwright's motion in 1891 was made about four months after the session opened, while this is made about two months after the session opened. That is convincing argument number one. Now, let us come to convincing argument number two-that in 1891 certain offensive allegations were made in a paper supporting the government of that day, while certain equally injurious statements have been made on this occasion in the press opposed to the government. Why, Mr. Speaker, as I understood my hon. friend from Algoma, his point was that in respect of all such matters there should be such perfect and absolute publicity that no paper in this country, Grit or Tory, would dare to utter even the breath of suspicion. It was only in that way that my hon. friend from Algoma alluded to the rumours in the press to-day, which have been contradicted, and I am willing and happy to accept the contradictions. But my right hon, friend was not ingenuous in dealing

with the position in 1891, because he forgot to mention to this House that the injurious statemeint, which he quoted in 1891, appeared in a certain newspaper in Montreal at a time when that journal was attacking the government, and when on one point at least it was actually opposed to the government and was trying to drive it out of power. When we make that qualification in the remarks of my right hon. friend, we shall see that there is really no distinction; and even if he had made his point, what has it to do, in the name of all that is reasonable and sensible, with the question before this House?
Now, I want to advert to some of the criticisms which have been made on the other side of the House upon the speech with which my hon. friend from Algoma introduced this resolution. There was evidently a pretty concerted arrangement to cast discredit and odium upon my hon. friend. One hon. gentleman referred to scavengers. I would like to ask that hon. gentleman, who were the scavengers in 1891? Because I am within the judgment of any hon. gentleman in this House who cares to examine carefully, as I have done more than once, the debate which took place in 1891, and who has listened to the speech of the hon. member for Algoma, as to whether that speech was not a more temperate and reasonable speech than that which was delivered by Sir Richard Cartwright in 1891; and there are rumours-I do not know whether they may be true or not-that Sir Richard Cartwright is not much more satisfied with the condition of affairs in 1911 than he was in 1891. My hon. friend from Algoma quoted copiously from the speeches of the Minister of Trade and Commerce and the right hon. gentleman who leads this House, and I leave it to the judgment of any one within hearing of my voice whether the quotations he gave from those speeches were not the severest portion of the remarks which he addressed to the House this afternoon. In my judgement they were. No other man, said the hon. member for South Grey (Mr. Miller), could have been found to introduce this resolution than the hon. member for Algoma. Well, I will tell the hon. member for South Grey something about that. If it had been a Conservative Finance Minister who had received this gift of $120,000 without any publication of the names of the contributors, I will tell my right hon. friend that two gentlemen, if they were in this House, would have been prepared to take that matter up. One of them is the Right Hon. Sir Wilfrid Lau-rier and the other is the Right Hon. Sir Richard Cartwright.
I listened with a great deal of interest to the statement of the Minister of Finance. I did not see any reason why 89
he should not have taken part in this debate in the ordinary sense, as his name was introduced only by reason of the incident to which I have referred. This resolution does not name him, and is not particularly concerned with him except with regard to the incident to which I have alluded, and because of the desire that parliament should establish a reasonable and salutary rule in this connection. My hon. friend, the Minister of Finance, made his statement. I accept absolutely, and not merely in a parliamentary sense, every word he said. I have been in pretty active opposition to him, in poli-,' tical life especially, during the past ten years, but I am perfectly willing to accord to him the tribute of having worked hard, and earnestly in the administration of his department, and I desire to cast no personal reflection upon him. But taking his statement to-day-if I may venture to pass an opinion upon his conduqt, which he has exposed to the House in a very frank way-I feel inclined to say that when he stipulated, or assented to the stipulation, that everything connected with the source of that fund should be shrouded in secrecy, he took a wrong course. The stipulation he should have made was that everything connected with the source of that fund should be, exposed to the utmost possible publicity.! In other words, the better-the only proper course-for him was to say: if you bring me a list of names which I can conscientiously accept, I will be willing to accept the testimonial these gentlemen, offer, but only upon the condition that the name of every one of the contributors shall be published in the press from one end of Canada to the other. That is the standard which the right hon. gentleman himself laid down in 1891. I am bound to say I could not quite understand why my hon. friend the Finance Minister should have desired these names to be kept secret, although I have carefully considered and analysed his statement and I desire to do him no injustice. He was willing, even desirous that the names should be made known to him later on, after his official career had terminated. Well, if the source of this fund was of the character demanded by the resolution of 1891, why should not the Finance Minister know the names now? As a matter of fact, every one of us knows, because we all have common sense, that ignorance with regard to the source of the contributions would in the future be absolutely impossible. In the case of the Finance Minister, holding the position he did, it would be idle for any of us to attempt to keep up the pretense that these contributions could be made and that the Finance Minister would not know who made them. The very idea



seems on the face of it utterly out of thq question. He was told that this money was to come from friends and admirers. Well, he would have a pretty shrewd idea as to who were his warmest friends and admirers, and it would be utterly preposterous to assume for one moment that he would not in the end have a pretty shrewd idea who these gentlemen were. So there could not be very much secrecy about it even if secrecy were desirable; and from the point of view taken in 1891 by the right hon. gentleman, .secrecy was the last thing to be desired.
My hon. friend from Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair) says that this list was a clean list. I have no knowledge, and therefore I do not for one moment gainsay his statement; but if it is a clean list, then it is a list that ought to be published. My hon. friend from Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair) said that this money was clean, money. Neither do I gainsay that statement," but if it was, why should not the names of the donors be published in the. press and laid upon the table of parliament? For what possible reason will it be proper for my hon. friend the Minister of Finance to know all these names, ten years hence after. he had passed out of official life, and yet not be proper for him to know them to-day, when he is holding an important position in the government, if this list be of the kind described?
Let us come to the debate of 1891 and( the terms of the resolution now before the House. My hon. friend from South Grey (Mr. Miller) thought it would be difficult to find any one in this House prepared to vote for this resolution. Well,
I would be surprised indeed if there were anything in this resolution that did not commend itself to every member of this House. Why, it is precisely on the same terms as the resolution of 1891, with this one addition. My right hon. friend (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) has characterized that addition as being couched in offensive terms. I fail to find any offence or even suspicion of offence in it; and in order to make my point good in that regard I shall read it to the House:
That in order to maintain this principle, the source of any gifts of money to any minister of the Crown ought not to be^ surrounded with secrecy, and that an authentic statement of the donors should he made public.
If there be anything offensive in that, it is my Tight hon. friend the Prime Minister who is the author of it, He gave the offence in 1891, and Sir Richard Cartwright gave it before 1891. It is all very well for my right hon. friend to deprecate passion and attack but he wras not so scrupulous in the old days. Inside of a couple of minutes I could bring to this House a volume Mr. BORDEN (Halifax).
of ' Hansard ' in which he declared that judges of the highest court in the province of Quebec had bought their places and that these men were making political contributions to the Conservative party. Respect for the judiciary has usually been inculcated in parliament and these men were not here to defend themselves. My right hon. friend was quite capable of hitting hard and quite willing to hit hard in the old days and he must not be too sensitive if some blows should pass across the floor of the House now, particularly when the severest of those blows comes in the very words which he used himself in 1891. He regards the speech of the hon. member for West Algoma (Mr. Boyce) as offensive. What did he think of his colleague Sir Richard Cartwright in 1891? He thought that he had made a splendid speech and had attained a notable triumph. What occupied more than one half of Sir Richard Cartwright's speech? [DOT] An attack on Sir John Macdonald, then only two months in his grave, in respect of a testimonial presented to him 15 or 18 years before. I have the report of some speeches made by ministers of the Crown as far back as 1877 and I find that even at that date the same colleague of my right hon. friend was raising questions about this matter. Here is what he then said in a speech delivered m the town of Simcoe on September 21, 1877, published by the Globe Printing and Publishing Company and used in the campaign of 1878, no doubt quoted by my right hon. friend the Prime Minister in the campaign he made in that year. He said:
Moreover, and it is a point of the very gravest importance as bearing on the conduct of all public men, I bold that it was Sir John Macdonald's duty not to have accepted, he being a public man, any testimonial unless everything connected with it was clear and above board, and capable of being published to all the world. That was his clear duty, and that he should have insisted on from the first Sir, I will not tolerate the poor pretence that he did not know who had subscribed to his testimonial. Before he took that money he should have taken care to prove that it came from 'clean hands, and that he could take it without a smirch on his. One hundred thousand dollars is no small gift, and Sir John knew-no man better-that the " very first principle of all agency is that no agent of any kind or degree has the smallest right to receive a present from any of his principal's customers or clients without the full knowledge of that principal. Sir John Macdonald was the agent of the people of Canada; he was a public man; be ought to have known better, and he did know better than to allow any testimonial to he presented to him without the fullest publicity attending it. Does this seem a harsh rule to impose on a public man's conduct? One moment's reflection will show you not only that it is most just, but most necessary and inexorable. Do away with this, and you throw wide the door for every kind and shape of bribery in

disguise. Do away with this and you may at once and forever blot out every law against tampering with the independence of parliament. (Hear, hear). Such testimonials, unless they are made publicly are, I repeat, a most dangerous precedent, one which no man is justified in accepting, and one which should not be permitted to be given by any people having a regard to their own interests. Well, Sir John M^tcdonald shut his eyes, and knowing only too well what sort of money would be taken to get up this testimonial, declined to investigate the matter, though he did not decline to receive the money.
I would point out to the Prime Minister that that was the tone of Sir Richard Cartwright's remarks and his own remarks all through the debate of 1891. If I might analyse what was said in that debate it amounts to this:	In the first place Sir
Richard Cartwright took the ground, he did not insist on it in the motion, but he did distinctly take the ground that no man in office ought to take gifts at all. I do not think that portion of his remarks has been quoted. He spoke at Ingersoll on November 14, 1889, and he regarded his remarks as so impressive and important that he repeated them in his speech in the House in 1891. He said:
Ministers should not take gifts. Now surely if there is any one maxim in political ethics better established than another, if there is any one thing which ought to commend itself to every honest man of every party in Canada, it is this: that under no circumstance should a minister of state permit himself to accept gifts, either directly or indirectly, while he continues in office.
And further on he said in the same speech:
If a man's political supporters do really desire to _ testify their administration by making him a gift of money let them wait till he is out of office, and then subscribe to their heart's content.
The same position was taken by the present Minister of Trade and Commerce in 1891. I am free to admit that it was not included in the resolution and that my right hon. friend the Prime Minister did not subscribe to it because in his speech he said that there might be circumstances under which the gift of a sum of money to a minister of the Crown would he a matter of credit not only to the men who presented it, but to the man who accepted it. There are two ideals, the higher and the lower. We have not attempted to put the higher ideal in our motion to-day. Sir Richard Cartwright did not attempt to put it iu his motion in 1891. We have been satisfied with putting in this motion the lower ideal but we have accompanied it with a clear statement of the necessity of publicity, which was insisted on by both Sir Richard Cartwright and the Prime Minister in the debate of 1891. That was the first standard which Sir Richard Cartwright set up but which he did not attempt to enforce by resolution. The second standard 89i	.
which Sir Richard Cartwright set up was that gifts ought not to be accepted from contractors or officials or any persons having pecuniary relations with the government. That was embodied in the resolution of 1891. It is also embodied in the resolution of to-day. Then the third principle which was put forward both by Sir Richard Cartwright and the right hon. the Prime Minister was not embodied in the resolution of 1891, but is embodied in the resolution of to-day. It is this ; that absolute and perfect publicity should attend all gifts of money or testimonials to ministers of the Crown. It does not seem to me to require very much argument to show that that position is absolutely good. How are the public of Canada to know, (and they have the right to know) that contractors, that officials, that persons having pecuniary relations with the government are not subscribers to this fund, unless you publish in the light of day, in the press of Canada, so that every man may know, the names of every man who has contributed to any such fund. It is absolutely impossible to work out the resolution of 1891, unless you adopt that principle which was a good principle in the judgment of the right hon. gentleman in 1891. Is it not a good principle in his judgment to-day ? If it is, why is it that he asks this House to vote it down? Further than that, my hon. friend, the Minister of Finance has defended himself against any suspicion in this matter by pleading that very ignorance and secrecy which my right hon. friend the Prime Minister denounced and which the Minister of Trade and Commerce denounced in 1891. The thing that these hon. gentlemen denounced in 1891 is the defence of the Minister of Finance to-day, yet my hon. friend the Prime Minister says that the defence of the Minister of Finance is an admirable one, is a defence to which no. hon. gentleman in this House can take the slightest exception. Let me repeat at the risk of wearying the House one or two of the strongest statements of opinion on this point, taken from Sir Richard Cartwright's speech.
Unfortunately these precautions were not taken, unfortunately publicity was not given as I have always said publicity should be given, to the names of persons who subscribed [DOT] and still more unfortunately precautions were not taken to see that subscriptions to that fund were not accepted save from sources from which they honourably could be accepted.
So right on through the speech of the Minister of Trade and Commerce, couched in the strongest possible terms, and directed with great force against the principle for which the right hon. gentleman stands to-day. The Prime Minister says that publicity is not necessary to-day. Whs' did he say in 1891?

The only thing, however, with which my hon. friend found fault in regard to what was done on that occasion by the friends of Sir John Macdonald was that instead of it being done publicly, as it should have been done, it was done in secret.
My hon. friend the Minister of Finance stood up before parliament and 'before the country to-day and stated that he stipulated, in connection with his testimonial, that there should be absolute and perfect secrecy with regard to it. I do not see how you can reconcile that statement of the Minister of Finance to-day with the statement in direct contradiction thereto made by the right hon. gentleman who leads the House when he spoke on that subject in 1891. But that is not all.
It may be wrong or it may be good, according to circumstances, but if such an act is done in the open light of day, then, Sir, it is the best prohibition that there can be against any wrong taking place. ,
What does that mean? That means that if there is absolute, perfect publicity, you have an absolute safeguard that no contractor, no official, no person having pecuniary interest with the government, is a subscriber to that fund. That is what the right hon. gentleman meant by that statement. Yet the Minister of Finance has told us that one of the main stipulations with regard to this fund was that the names of the subscribers should be kept an absolute secret. Then the Prime Minister went on :
If the hon. gentleman did not know, it was because he chose to remain ignorant of who were the names on the list, and if he chose to be ignorant of the names which were on that list, is it not because his moral sense told him that he might there find names of persons giving contributions which should not he accepted at all?
I hardly like to read the strictures of the right hon. gentleman in 1891, because they come home with so much force to us today in view of the statement that was made this afternoon iby his colleague whose name has been brought up in connection with these matters. Further on :
Certainly there could he nothing wrong in the admirers of a man in public life coming to his help and rescuing him; but it seems to me that the recipient of such favours would naturally he too glad to know who are the persons to whom he owes gratitude, and if he does not chose to know who are those to . whom he owes gratitude, it must be because his moral sense tells him that he would find there names which would be a condemnation of his accepting such a testimonial.
Is there anything in the remarks of my hon. friend from Algoma to-day approaching in severity the quotation I have just read from the Prime Minister in addressing this House in 1891? Mr. Speaker, were these principles sincerely held by the Mr. BORDEN (Halifax).
Prime Minister in 1891 or not? Does he withdraw from them to-day, or say that they are not as good now as he deemed them to be in 1891? He has not told us so to-night. This list is a clean list, according to the statement of the hon. member for Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair). Is there any reason that the Prime Minister can assign, that any hon. gentleman can assign, why it should not be published? I have heard none from any gentleman on the other side of the House, from any gentleman who has spoken to-day. I have heard no reason whatever why this list should not be published. The people haxm the right to read it and to form their own conclusions. Assuming, as I do, the statement of my hon. friend the Minister of Finance to be an absolutely true and frank statement with regard to this whole transaction, I say that it affords the best possible reason why that list should he published to the people of Canada without one hour's delay.
Now just one word in conclusion. My right hon. friend has struggled manfully, but in vain, to find some reason why the government would be justified in refusing to accept this amendment. My hon. friend from Algoma has stated that he does not present it as a vote of want of confidence. He follows in that respect the course which was adopted by the present Minister of Trade and Commerce in 1891. The resolution contains no charge against any Minister of the Crown, it contains no reflection upon any Minister of the Crown, it ;s purely and simply a recital, a renewed declaration of a principle agreed on by both sides of the House in 1891. It contains further a statement of principle, of public importance, and even necessity which was put forward in 1891 as an absolutely necessary accompaniment to the resolution passed in that year. My right hon. friend considers this amendment as a resolution of want of confidence. The hon. member for Algoma says that he does not present it in that view. The government call upon their followers to vote it. down. They have accepted within the past ten years at least ten motions proposed in amendment to Committee of Supply, which were quite as much motions of want of confidence as the one now proposed. The government are asked to accept the principle of 1891, together with a further principle which is an absolutely necessary accompaniment and corollary thereto, without which the principle affirmed in the resolution of 1891 becomes easy of evasion and cannot be carried out. Two standards were set up by the then Minister of Trade and Commerce. He set up the standard that no gifts of any kind should be made to Ministers of the Crown. We are not going that far to-day. 1 He set up a second standard, that no gifts

from contractors, no gifts from.officials, no gifts from persons having pecuniary relations with the government, should be accepted. He laid down a third principle, strongly affirmed also by the Prime Minister, that no gifts should be accepted, although they came from absolutely untainted^ sources, unless those gifts were accompanied by the utmost possible publicity in respect of the sources from, which the contributions came. A regard for the proper standards of public life demands that the resolution of 1891 should, be reaffirmed to-day, not only in the form which it took then, which was agreed to by both sides of the House, but in the form now presented by my hon. friend from Al-goma, namely, that any such contributions if made to ministers of the Crown must in the first place come from absolutely clean and untainted sources, and in the second place, those sources should be disclosed fully, and without the slightest attempt at concealment or evasion, to the parliament of Canada, and to the people of this country.

maintopic: SUPPLY-MR. J. A. MACDONALD AND RECIPROCITY.
subtopic: TESTIMONIALS TO MINISTERS OF THE CROWN.
speechtext:
I do not know that I can add much to this debate, but some remarks have fallen from the lips of the leader of the opposition with which I have to take direct issue. The hon. member seems to think that because the mover of this resolution said that he did not introduce it as a motion of want of confidence we must absolutely ignore the linking up with it of the name of the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding), and the well known facts with regard to the subscription to a testimonial to that minister, and the methods, manner and language in which this motion was moved. I may say frankly at once that as far as the substance of this motion is concerned I have no quarrel with it. I would not oppose in any way a substantive resolution which should propose to advance this House farther than it went in 1891. But, when a resolution comes as an attack upon the honour and integrity of a member of the government whose reputation and character are far above attack in this country and beyond the confines of this country I cannot recognize this motion as anything but a deliberate motion of want of confidence in the government, because it undertakes to asperse the character and integrity of one of the most important members of the government. Mere words to say that that is not the meaning of it are ineffective and useless in face of the tone and character of the speech of the hon. member (Mr. Boyce) who introduced the resolution. If he had desired to make this a simple declaration of the parliament of Canada involving what is included in the words of this resolution why did he make the motion as a result of
his inquiries and his statements of a few days ago in parliament as to the subscription of Mr. Travers to the Fielding fund? Why was this the result of that? Why was it introduced at a time when the Minister of Finance himself should be present if it were not aimed at the Minister of Finance? It is not a motion enunciating a general principle, but it is a direct and violent attack upon the honour of a member of the government, upon the honour of the leader of the Liberal party, and I think that the right hon. leader of the government (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) and the leader of this House was well within his rights in calling upon those who have confidence in Mr. Fielding to vote down this resolution. The hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Borden, Halifax) quotes deliberately and at considerable length from the excellent speech of the gentleman who introduced the resolution in 1891, and he undertakes to say that the Liberal party has gone back on its principles then enunciated and has changed its stand. He does not say anything about a change of stand by his friends of the Conservative party. I suppose he is so accustomed to such changes that he does not think them wonderful, but if the Liberals do change their front in any way it is open to objection.

maintopic: SUPPLY-MR. J. A. MACDONALD AND RECIPROCITY.
subtopic: TESTIMONIALS TO MINISTERS OF THE CROWN.
speechtext: Is that meant to be sarcastic?

maintopic: SUPPLY-MR. J. A. MACDONALD AND RECIPROCITY.
subtopic: TESTIMONIALS TO MINISTERS OF THE CROWN.
speechtext:
No, it is only the plain truth without any sarcasm in it. I will just ppint out what was the origin of the debate in 1891, and I shall quote the few words with which Sir Richard Cartwright introduced the motion. I shall not read the resolution because it has been read already several times, but this is what Sir Richard Cartwright said distinctly and clearly:
This motion declares, Sir-and let this be carefully remembered-this motion does not object to and does not censure the acceptance of gifts or testimonials by ministers of the Crown from their political or personal ad mirers, unless, indeed, these parties should belong to classes having direct pecuniary relations with the government at the time. Such a proposition, it appears to me, ought to commend itself to every right-feeling and right-thinking man from one end of this Dominion to the other, and I go further; it ought to commend itself to every honest man and to every right-thinking man under every constitutional government. There could be, in my judgment, no proposition clearer or plainer than this. There could be no one thing which tends more to the interest of good government, and which is more vital to the proper management 0f the public service than laying down once and for all the declaration on the part of this parliament: That it is not expedient that ministers of the Crown should accept from persons who may appear before them in the guise of suitors, from per-

sons in regard to whom they stand in position of judges, any gifts or presents of testimonials of any kind or description. I repeat again, Sir, that I am not raising the vexed question as to whether a minister of the Crown should or should not accept gifts during his term of office from political admirers. That, I have always held, is a matter of opinion, and it must be determined by the peculiar circumstances in each case.

speechtext: My hon. friends may laugh and interrupt and they are welcome to read on if they desire to do so. But, I want to point out that the declaration which is contained in the first part of this motion and the declaration of Sir Richard Cartwright when he moved it was a distinct declaration that it was aimed at the acceptance of gifts from contractors, from those who were receiving favours from the minister and from the government and not in regard to gifts of those who were political or personal friends. That is the difference between the situation then and the situation to-day.

speechtext: Oh, oh.

maintopic: SUPPLY-MR. J. A. MACDONALD AND RECIPROCITY.
subtopic: TESTIMONIALS TO MINISTERS OF THE CROWN.
speechtext: Hon. members laugh and say, what is the difference? The difference is this, that at that time Sir Richard Cartwright was aiming at a testimonial which had been given to Sir Hector Lange-vin at a time when everybody, as well as the public press, including the Conservative press, had declared that Sir Hector Langevin was receiving gifts from the contractors in his own department, and when Sir Hector Langevin had been obliged to leave the Conservative government because of mal-administration in his office had been proved against him, mal-administration which shortly afterwards drove him out of public life The conditions and the circumstances are entirely different from the position of to-day.

maintopic: SUPPLY-MR. J. A. MACDONALD AND RECIPROCITY.

speechtext: What about the principles-are they different?

maintopic: SUPPLY-MR. J. A. MACDONALD AND RECIPROCITY.
subtopic: TESTIMONIALS TO MINISTERS OF THE CROWN.
speechtext: The principles are the same but the circumstances and the facts are not the same, and principles should apply when the facts are the same and only then. Nobody declares or for a moment suggests that Mr. Fielding has received a favour or a gift from any man whom he has favoured in his public administration of the affairs of this country.

speechtext:
Does the hon. gentleman state that to his knowledge the names of no contractors or other persons having Mr. FISHER.
pecuniary relations with the government appear on the list of contributors to this testimonial?

subtopic: TESTIMONIALS TO MINISTERS OF THE CROWN.
speechtext: I do not state it from my personal knowledge, but I have no hesitation in stating it because I know that the committee that had charge of the testimonial was composed of honourable men, that they accepted the trust which they undertook at the request of Hon. Mr. Fielding on that distinct understanding and only on that understanding would he allow them to proceed with the work and allow them to give him a testimonial. Hon. gentlemen opposite shrug their shoulders.

maintopic: SUPPLY-MR. J. A. MACDONALD AND RECIPROCITY.

speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: SUPPLY-MR. J. A. MACDONALD AND RECIPROCITY.
subtopic: TESTIMONIALS TO MINISTERS OF THE CROWN.
speechtext: Yes, my hon. friend opposite says ' hear, hear.' I regret to think that there are men who have such a low opinion of the honour and integrity of their fellow citizens and of those who stand high in commercial, banking and other positions in Canada, who stand high in the life of this country, and who have declared solemnly and absolutely that _ there is no man who has that relation with the government who has made a subscription to this testimonial. I am prepared for one to accept that declaration and, I am prepared for one to believe that the friends of Mr. Fielding who surrounded him were sufficiently imbued with his own high honour and integrity to know that if they did that, notwithstanding the conditions which had been laid down by Mr. Fielding, they would be guilty of the basest betrayal of the friendship and confidence of a public man. I do not believe that the committee have said a word that- is untruthful or that they would be so unfaithful to the trust that they had accepted. I am sorry for my hon. friend opposite that he cannot have that faith in human nature.

speechtext: Will the hon. gentleman (Mr. Fisher), kindly explain what that has to do with the principle declared in that resolution ?

maintopic: SUPPLY-MR. J. A. MACDONALD AND RECIPROCITY.
subtopic: TESTIMONIALS TO MINISTERS OF THE CROWN.
speechtext:
It has a gcod deal to do with the facts; it has a good deal to do with comparisons between the conditions in 1891 and the conditions in 1910. Arid the whole circumstances, as Sir Richard Cartwright said, when he introduced that resolution, are left to the opinion and judgment of the minister who receives the aiftfrom his personal friends and admirers. And so it is in this Case with Mr. Fielding. Mr. Fielding is reproached because he stipulated for secrecy, and his words and his position are contrasted with those of the right hon. Prime Minister (Sir Wilfrid Laurier), who, in 1891, expressed the opinion that secrecy was inadvisable. There is a difference of opinion. The leader | of the opposition (Mr. Borden, Halifax),

said a few minutes ago that if he were to make a criticism of Mr. Fielding at all it. would be because his judgment had allowed him to stipulate for secrecy. There is a difference of opinion and of conduct between two men. I confess that I sympathize a great deal with -Mr. Fielding's desire not to know the names of the men who were contributing to this present, so that, if, in future, any of these men happen to have relations with him, he might not be hampered in dealing with them by the fact that in a day gone by, they had com tributed to a testimonial for his benefit. But that does not in any way acknowledge or pretend, nor should anybody think, that, at the moment that testimonial was made, they had or expected to have any., relations with the government. When this testimonial was arranged for, what was the *declaration of parliament ? It was only the first part of this resolution. This Mr. Fielding knew, and he stipulated that it should be fulfilled to the letter. Mr. Fielding's friends accepted and acted upon and within, not the law of the land, I grant you, but the resolution and opinion of parliament which has the right to give its opinion upon such questions. Let me remind hon. gentlemen opposite that if the right hon. leader (Sir Wilfrid Laurier), expressed an opinion in 1891 that secrecy was inadvisable,. and if Sir Richard Cartwright said the same, the House of Commons at that time, did not accept that view, did not insert that in the resolution, but simply passed the first part of the present resolution and left it there, thus dealing only with the question of those having relations with the government subscribing to testimonials.
Now, I wish to say a word with regard to another phase of this question. Mr. Fielding's name has been forced into this discussion, and none of us can in any way look upon this motion except in regard to Mr. Fielding. I say that frankly, and 1 say that that is the reason why I, personally, feel bound to vote down the resolution, because it is a direct attack and aspersion upon a man who as my colleague, I have known intimately, whom I know to be absolutely above reproach and whose character is such, that I am ashamed of the men who dare to make insinuations of this kind against him.

speechtext:
I was proceeding to another aspect of this question, upon which I would like to say a few words. Mr. Fielding has received a testimonial from friends and admirers of a large sum of money. There is no doubt that the reason for this testimonial- is that Mr. Fielding, through a long period of public service, has given activities and mental qualities to the public service to an extent which has prevented him from laying up proper provision for his own old age and for the proper provision for his family. He has done this, as we all know, through more than twenty-five years of public service. I make the deliberate statement that he has done this for twenty-five years of public service of the highest character which, in the salaries he has received in the whole of these twenty-five years, have been absolutely inadequately rewarded or paid for. Mr. Fielding was for twelve years-speaking from memory-the Prime Minister of the province of Nova Scotia. I do not know exactly what he received through all that administration, but I think that during part of it he received $5,000 a year, I have no hesitation in saying that having to perform the duties of the Prime Minister's position in a province of Canada and having to fulfil the social obligations of that position and to live in accord-

281S
ance with the position ; having a family depending upon him and being obliged to bring up that family in a way commensurate with the associates of that family while he occupied that position, and being called upon to meet the immense number of calls upon his charity and upon his public spirit which always go with a position of that kind-it was positively and -absolutely impossible for Mr. Fielding to have made any savings or any provision for the future of himself or his family.
For the last fourteen years and more Mr. Fielding has been Finance Minister for the Dominion of Canada. We all know what salary he has received-$7,000 a year. Now, Mr. Speaker, I think I can speak with a certain freedom, because being a bachelor my salary is sufficient for my needs. I speak advisedly, and I speak in all seriousness, when I say that for my needs the salary I have received during the last fourteen years has been sufficient-I will go further and say, with no surplus left at the end of the year. But I venture to say-and I say it so that it may be heard through all this House, and I hope it will be remarked throughout the Dominion of Canada that the salary which a minister of the Crown receives in Ottawa, if he lives according to the position he occupies, if he spends money in the way in which those with whom he has to associate spend their money, is not adequate to the demands upon his purse if he has a family and if he is expected to lay by a provision for his old age and to make provision for his family. When Canada undertakes to so pay her ministers of the Crown that they cannot make such provision, there is only one other way in which those men can be honourably helped if they have sacrificed their lives and their health in the public service, and that way is, if they have no fortune of their own, no resources to fall back upon, for friends and admirers to come to their assistance and relieve them from the anxieties and worries necessarily attendant upon the life of any man who has a family dependent upon him, and who has not made provision for them in case of accident to himself. I say further, that Mr. Fielding's devotion to his public duties, as, we know only too sadly, has to a large extent broken down his health, we trust and believe only temporarily; but, at the same time, when a man reaches the age which ' he has reached, and has not made the proper provision for an older age and for his family's future, it is a cause of worry and anxiety. This in most cases, in any man not so devoted to the public service as Mr. Fielding, would render it very difficult indeed for him to perform the full measure of his public duty, and I say that a public service to the Dominion Mr. FISHER.
of Canada has been rendered by those who subscribed to this Fielding testimonial if by reason of that fact Mr. Fielding is able the better and for a longer time te continue that splendid seivice for his country which he has performed for the past twenty-five years. That is a debt of gratitude which the people of Canada owe to the subscribers to that testimonial, and I am satisfied that the people throughout the length and breadth of this Dominion will acknowledge that debt of gratitude, and will repudiate the accusations which have been made against those subscribers just as much as against the recipient of that testimonial.

speechtext:
Perhaps too sensitive. I can appreciate that my hon. friend cannot sympathize with that at all; but I thank God that we have some men in public life in Canada who are sensitive. I appreciate the fact that there are men-and I am glad to be able to say that they are not confined to one party, but that there are a large number of Conservatives-who are sensitive in regard to their public reputation and their record in public affairs, and are therefore careful of their utterances and their actions, and for that reason are the better men-the better Conservatives

if you like, but certainly the better citizens and the better Canadians.
I have said these few things, Sir, to show not. only to those within the sound of my voice, but to others, that there is a reason and in many cases a necessity, for friends and admirers to step in and do something for public men who have not wealth at their command; and that is only one of the reasons why a resolution such as this should not go very much further and say that it should be impossible in Canada for men in office to receive anything in the way of gift, testimonial or anything else. But in the condition of affairs which I have briefly described, I conceive that there are conditions and circumstances in individual cases where that is the only recourse to save for the country the continued work and effort of those great men who are thus circumstanced, and the only way in which they can be relieved of the anxiety and the worry which is natural to the father of a family and the husband of a wife. I regret that this motion has been brought forward in the way in which it has been. If hon. gentlemen opposite had wanted to lay down a principle in regard to the future of the public life of Canada, they should have done what the right hon. the leader of the House suggested-brought forward a substantive motion, and at a time when it would have no personal application, without dragging the name of either subscriber or recipient into the discussion. And then I believe that we might have been able to put upon the records of this House a resolution which would have been advantageous to the public credit of the country and be accepted unanimously and thereby, and only thereby, have that force which must be behind any resolution put or carried.

speechtext:
I do not propose to detain the House very long in the few remarks I am about to make on this question. Neither do I propose to argue it in a personal manner at all. I think there is a great principle involved in the resolution before the House, and just at this moment I am a little in trouble as to the fate of that principle if the determination of the Prime Minister is carried out, and the House votes it down. The right hon. gentleman says that we have to-day a rule or law of parliament in existence, that rule and law being the resolution which was passed in 1891, and which forbids gifts to ministers of the Crown by contractors or persons interested. Well, if that be a rule and law of parliament and a good one, established . by the assent of both parties in 1891, and one which the Prime Minister himself then most vehemently supported, what are we going to have in its place after a vote on this resolution is taken and the right hon. the
Prime Minister, through his majority in this House, abrogates that rule and law, negatives it, and leaves nothing in its place? I think that is rather a serious condition especially in view of the fact that the right hon. gentleman's colleague (Mr. Fisher) who has just sat down has elucidated and given governmental sanction to an absolutely untenable and vicious principle. I would ask my right hon. friend the leader of the House, if he will subscribe to that. What is that principle? It is that whenever a man who is a minister of the Crown is unable to take care of his wife and children and bring them up according to the conditions of the life in which he moves, whenever he is unable to do this and meet his other expenses, his friends and admirers are in duty bound to come to his rescue and make him a gift of 8100,000 or so. That is a direct invitation to gift making and establishes a vicious principle-a vicious principle which I do not believe the right hon. the Prime Minister himself will stand for. It is a direct invitation to every minister in the present cabinet to come along with a statement of his finances, and show that ho is not able to meet the demands upon him, that he has to spend so much on his family, that he has to give out so much to charity, and that he has to meet besides certain other furbelows and functions, and finds his salary insufficient; and then, on this appeal, two or three or more of his friends get together and start a foraging expedition and find subscriptions enough from his supporters to deposit the comfortable sum of $100,000 or so to his credit in the bank for his personal use and gratification. If there is anything in that statement of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Fisher), that is the principle involved in it. Does the right hon. gentleman stand by that? Oh, but it is urged, Mr. Fielding is poor and he is honest. Well, what about the other members of the cabinet Are any of them poor? I do not know. Will the Prime Minister draw a distinction between the Finance Minister and the other members of his cabinet? The Finance Minister is honest, but are any of the others dishonest? By what rule, now that you have started and given sanction to the principle as stated by the Minister of Agriculture, can you treat the others differently? Take the case of any other minister, whose friends want to stand well with him, what is to prevent them taking the same course with regard to him? Oh, but the Prime Minister was fine tonight when he was saying that publicity was the very groundwork and guarantee of ministerial honesty in this matter. Publicity, he said, was the modern requirement and the principal requirement, and in this connection everything was done in public. There was a banquet, there wrere speeches and a presentation-the elements

of publicity were absolutely complied with and there was a guarantee of the greatest amount of honesty underlying the whole business. It was fine-no doubt about it- almost as fine as that other flight of his in, this direction. In 1891, it was all right to bring in-not a motion in condemnation of Sir Hector Langevin for no such motion was brought in by the right hon. gentleman at that time-but a general motion affirming a general principle. The argument of the right hon. gentleman then went to show that the resolution was not specially directed against Sir Hector Langevin, but a general one affirming a general principle which became the law, and rule of this House. In what manner was that resolution introduced? It was introduced on a motion to go into Supply, made by myself who was then Finance Minister, and it affirmed a general principle. In the discussion which took place, language was used by the right hon. gentleman himself and his colleagues which was not all honey and balm, and which would compare favourably for strength and vigour with the statment of my hon. friend from Algoma (Mr. Boyce),.but the resolution was the affirmation of a general principle, and in that sense it was adopted. Sir John Thompson, who . was then leader of the government said: This is introduced on the motion to go into Supply, but it is the affirmation of a general principle in which we agree and therefore we shall assent to it, and join in passing it. But Sir John Thompson reminded the right hon. gentleman and his colleagues that while he assented to that resolution as being the affirmation of a general principle, he did not at all endorse the very strong and emphatic language used by Sir Richard Cartwright, and my right hon. friend. But he did not make such a childish plea as to say that because the man who introduced that general resolution wore a gray coat instead of a black one, he therefore would oppose it and treat it as a want of confidence motion.
But the right hon. gentleman and his worthy colleague (Mr. Fisher) who has just taken his seat go a little further. The right hon. gentleman says : I agree with the first part of the resolution, I am willing to affirm it, I will not affirm the latter part. I am not sure whether he agreed with it or not but it is his own language, the very identical words that he used in 1891, not on a special matter but on a general principle. But the right hon. gentleman has so often disagreed with himself that he would feel out of-common atmosphere, and some way leading off from the general tendency of his life if he agreed just once with the language of which he was formerly the father and the sponsor. But he says this is the reason why he treats it as a motion Mr. FOSTER.
of want of confidence. If my hon. friend (Mr. Boyce) had waited two months more and then 'brought it in in the very same way, he would not have treated it as a motion of want of confidence, it makes a difference as to the date of the month on which a general principle is affirmed as to whether it is right for him to support it. My hon. friend the Minister of Agriculture goes a step further. He not only agrees with the first part tout he agrees with the second part. The whole resolution is absolutely right in the eyes of the Minister of Agriculture. But he has to vote against it. He ranges around the back part of his head to find out what strong reasons can be got up which will fortify him in his statement that although he agrees with it he will not vote for it. What are the reasons that he brings in? Because he believes Mr. Fielding is an honest man, and that this is an attack on Mr. Fielding. Is it any more an attack on Mr. Fielding than the very wording of the original resolution in 1891 was an attack upon Sir Hector Langevin? To-night, Mr. Fielding has not been attacked, he has been used, I think, with great magnanimity, and with great courtesy by the members on this side of the House, a magnanimity and courtesy which were absolutely wanting in 1891 with reference to both Sir Hector Langevin and Sir John A. Macdonald. But the minister, astute reasoner, logician from the early days, has to-night made the unparalleled record, reached the apex of all logical reasoning, and declares that he agrees with every word and line in the whole resolution, which is a general resolution, and the affirmation of a general principle, but will vote against it because he conceives that it might be construed into an attack on the Finance Minister. There are two able gentlemen, one the leader of the party, and the other his able and astute lieutenant. There are their statements as to the resolution, and there are the reasons why they must vote against it. Might I invite my right hon. friend to take that resolution and show in the second part of it one single offensive word. I shall read it, and shall leave it to Mr. Speaker to point out to this House the offensive word.
That in order to maintain this principle the sources of any gifts of money to ministers of the Grown ought not to he surrounded with secrecy, and that an authentic statement of the names of the donors should forthwith be made public.
Mr. Speaker, where is the offensive word? Might I ask my right hon. friend to point out the offensive word or line. Will he do it? That is the only objection the right hon. gentleman has to that part of it. Although it is made as an amendment to go into Supply he is willing to go so far as to adopt the first part and let it run in as a

motion of want of confidence, but he will not adopt the second, his own identical words, because he says it is offensive, and he will not point out to the House a single offensive word or phrase in that resolution. I commend these two hon. gentlemen, not to the tender mercies of this House, they always have them, but to the tender consideration of the public which will wake up to-morrow morning and at its breakfast table read these two weighty arguments *and reasons of these two weighty men. I remember very well 1891, I remember the whole debate and I remember the occasion. At that time, the Liberal-Conservatives met these gentlemen in spite of their strictures and their partisan attacks and said yes, looking at the past, knowing what has been done, we agree now with you on that side *of the House, we all agree to a general rule and law of action which shall bind us in the future. Who has broken this contract? This side of the House has never broken it, this side of the House stands by it to-day, and to-day, when that law is.violated, we ask hon. gentlemen opposite to join with us and reaffirm the general law and rule, we ask them for the sake of the public life of Canada not to remove the salutary law which is at the present the law of parliament, as they say they intend to do, and leave this whole thing wide open, more especially with that wicked principle enunciated .by the Minister of Agriculture, a call to the faithful, to contractors that are and contractors that are to be, lookers for favours for the present and for the future, to come to the assistance of every minister whose salary is not sufficient to keep his house running and his expenses paid. With respect to this $120,000 given with all the guarantees of publicity that have been so eloquently described hy the right hon. gentleman to-night, the Prime Minister has sung as the refrain of his argument to the House and to the country: Will any one say that a word can be brought against the honour of William Fielding? The Minister of Agriculture beat out another and a little different refrain, but for the same reason, that he has given long and faithful services, and is poor. If they have thrown that before the House, it is not my fault if I comment upon it. My comment is simply this, that of all public men in Canada, I do not think you can pick out another whose position in a monetary point of view, in payment for services to the state, compares with that of the Finance Minister of this day. I make that statement, why do I make it? Mr. Fielding had not stepped out of private life into public life until he had a government position with its salary assured to him. Mr. Fielding has not passed one hour of his life from that time up to the present that he has not been a member of a government in receipt of a government salary. My right hon. friend has not had an experience like that. He fought some time before he got into the House. He got in, and he stayed in but a little while, and again he fought for many a long year in the cold shades of opposition. When he came in again in 1896 lie did the work, but he enjoyed the emoluments of the office, the emoluments that this country has said is all that a man should receive from the master to the servant. But, Sir, there is not another example in the history of politics in this country showing so favourable a position as that of the hon. gentleman who is Finance Minister to-day.
Now I will tell you exactly the feeling that ran through me this afternoon when my hon. friend was making his statement; it was a feeling of pity, of absolute pity that any country as rich as Canada is, and any parliament as sensible as this parliament is, would run the risk of throwing its public servants to the tender mercies of contractors and seekers from the government for a provision which they refused to pay them. It is pitiable, Sir, and it no credit to this government nor to this country. I tell you, Mr. Speaker, plainly that if the proposition had been made, and the circumstances set out, and the government had come down to this House last year with this proposition or an alternative: Vote to the Hon. Wm. Fielding $100,000, or turn him over in his old age to the mercy of contractors-I would have voted, cheerfully voted, to pay him the $100,000. What are the circumstances, even in this case? The Finance Minister did not want to know and he does not know, the Minister of Agriculture, whether he wants to know or not, does not know, the right hon. gentleman who leads this House does not know whether the stipulations made by Mr. Fielding have'been carried out or not. The stipulations were right in their way. Where is the evidence that the stipulations have been carried out as they were made? You will never satisfy public opinion, and you will never clear the Minister of Finance or the government, until you place in the possession of the people the evidence of that which you declare is true. The' people of this country are not fools, they are sensible, and the man upon the street, and the man in the club, and the man everywhere will say: What in the world is all the trouble about? If the subscriptions are all right, who is ashamed of them? Are the donors ashamed that they have done so philanthropic an act as the Minister of Agriculture has described to us to-night? I do not think so. Are the donors ashamed that they should be known as public spirited citizens who had come to the aid of a government which is too miserly to make a living provision to its own working Finance Minister? I do not think so. Who would

be harmed, if that list is all right and the stipulations have been carried out, if the list were placed before the people of this country whose servants you and we are?
My view of it is this, and I challenge the Prime Minister to say that it is not the British view and the right view, that no minister of the Crown whilst he is in office, or when he is out of office with an expectation of coming back again in to office, ought to put himself into the position of taking gifts of any kind. That has to be modified only by some great emergent conditions, where a man has met with some disaster, where he has been borne down by hard luck, calamity, sickness and the like of that. I can conceive that a circumstance might arise when his friends might come to his aid. But I am speaking on general principles. Sir, to-day in Great Britain-though I think it may be that in some respects the grade is not quite so high there as it used to be, I will not say that dogmatically-but I say that no British minister could stand for a single hour in parliament with a gift of $120,000 in his pocket, nor with a gift of $10,000 in his pocket. He could not do it, it is un-British, and it is un-British for the best of reasons, that it is unsound as a maxim of public political life that such a thing should be allowed. Sir Richard Cartwright, with all his bitterness of invective and all his strength of expression, is pretty sound upon those constitutional points, and the statement that was read by the leader of the opposition to-night made by Sir Richard was concise, and true, and sane, and healthy, that no minister of the Crown should take gifts while he is in office.
Now I ask again the question which the common people will ask: If this thing is all right, why not let everybody know it. But one thing seems to have escaped the discussion to-night. There are some men that the Minister of Finance does know were interested in it. There are some men whose names are out in the open light of day; we have four of them mentioned to-night, two of them self-confessed, the other two given by the organ of the party-the ' Globe.' No one doubts that the hon. member for Grey (Mr. Miller) and the hon. member for Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair), Mr.- Jaffray, the senator, and Mr. Larkin, the party leader and the party supplier of large campaign funds, were the head and front of it. The Finance Minister knows that. Some of those men are before him every day for favours. The hon. member for Grey is before him every day for favours. The hon. member for Guysborough is before him every day for favours and the minister knows that they engineered the funds and that without that engineering he never would have had it. There is an instance, patent to everybody of the violation of the principle, if there ever was Mr. FOSTER.
any principle at all, in the resolution which the right hon. leader of the government in 1891 was so ardent an advocate of.
Now, I will say this in conclusion. I find that the little notes I have .taken are all gone over with the exception of one-I have not prepared a speech, but I have just taken up some points that occurred to me. But. there is one that I think it would hardly be fair for me to let go entirely by. There was a remark made by the Minister of Agriculture, who declared that he was a sensitive politician. Then he thought that he said a wonderful thing when he said that there were sensitive politicians on that side of the House and he must thank God for it. So he was a sensitive politician, he said, and he thanked God that there were some sensitive politicians. The Minister of Agriculture is a sensitive politician when lie is asked to vote for a resolution which he acknowledges to be right, but when he wants to vote against it he is not so sensitive then. There might be some shadow of a shade of an implication against the Minister of Finance and his sensitive soul will not allow him to envisage such possibilities and contingencies as that. Oh, would to God that same sensitiveness would suffuse the sou] of the Minister of Agriculture and his colleagues in the case of the multitudinous mal-administration which has been exposed in this House by the opposition and sustained by hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House. What I pray for, if my prayers go any distance at all

speechtext:
Hear, hear.
Mr. FOSTER-and I will invite the hon. Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham), who looks serious enough just at this moment, to join with me in those prayers, is that a little more sensitiveness of conscience may be imparted to the members of the administration from the Prime Minister down to the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Pugsley) when those awful things are exposed to the House and when that publicity which is the guardian and the guarantee of private and public life sp eulogized by the Prime Minister to-night is fought for by this side and the door is banged and bolted on the other side of the House.
But, I am not going to leave this discussion without bringing forward just one further thought, and it is this: Outside of this particular instance as it affects the office and as it affects the man in the office and the canons of public and private life, there is a very grave consideration which none of us, I am sure, will leave out of account. It is the power of example. Of all men in the whole public service, that man who ought to be the most careful, that man who ought to be the most circumspect, that man who ought to avoid the least suspicion or comment is the min-

ister of the department and the minister of the government who is to set an example to the whole public service and to the public life of this country. What would we think to-morrow morning if the customs collector in the port of Montreal, were to have had a meeting of his friends and admirers in the city of Montreal, and they had subscribed a testimonial of $50,000, had had a banquet and had all this beautiful publicity, tout had failed to give the names of the subscribers and it went out through the length and breadth of this country that the collector of customs in the port of Montreal had received gifts from his friends and admirers ? What would the public opinion say ? Is it not proper for me, knowing the collector of customs in Montreal, to say, that, in my opinion, he is not rich and that he is honest? If, because a man is poor and honest in the case of a minister of the Crown is a reason why the sound canons of political morality should be violated, what reason is there that the collector of customs, a sub-officer under the Crown, should not take from his friends and admirers, on the ground that he is poor and honest, a testimonial, because this is the sange reason as that which is given why .ministers should accept it ? If the Minister of Finance may take $120,000 from his friends and admirers, why cannot the Minister of Public Works take $120,000 from his friends and admirers ? But I will venture this that if to-morrow morning the news went out through this country that the friends and admirers of the Minister of Public Works had given him a secret donation of $100,000 there would be ructions in this country. When the example is set, when the principle is formed and the practise is laid down in the case of one minister of the Crown, how are you going to prevent other ministers of the Crown from following it, and in exactly the same way the pernicious influence goes through the whole service and permeates the whole country. Your sub-officer or under officer, if you may speak of him as such, says:	Well, the high muck-a-mucks take
these gifts from their friends and admirers because they are poor and honest* I am poor-mighty poor-and I am just as honest as they are; why cannot I take a little gift on the side too, without any unnecessary publicity ?
I have not the least doubt in the world that demoralization, swift and sure, along the whole _ line follows this unfortunate movement in the wrong direction. To-night we find the Prime Minister with his party behind him, and this latest advocate closing the debate on that side, declaring that it is perfectly right for ministers of the Crown to take gifts if only they are poor and honest. Have any other members of the government taken gifts?-(Don't all speak at once!)-
Is the Prime Minister a sinner in that respect? Would that make his feelings kind towards the Minister of Finance? Are any other ministers in similar positions for lesser sums?
